These include multipurpose community centres for women, grants to Zilla Parishads for Mahila Mandals, grants for Devadasi rehabilitation hostels in Kolhapur and Sangli, and provision of solar power sets to anganwadi centres.The solar power scheme has been replaced by assistance for electricity bills, said the order.The Majhi Kanya Bhagyashree scheme, replaced by the Lek Ladki Yojana, will be closed after pending claims up to March 2027 are settled.Schemes providing assistance to shelter homes under Aadhar Gruha and financial aid to orphans affected by the COVID-19 pandemic will be phased out by FY 2027-28 due to overlapping central schemes or absence of fresh applications, the order said.The Women and Child Welfare Department said the move was aimed at avoiding duplication, improving resource utilisation and taking into account demand, availability of alternative schemes, implementation status and budgetary provisions, and did not mean an across-the-board discontinuation of services.The seven schemes reviewed include multipurpose social centres for women, grants to women's groups, financial assistance for rehabilitation of children of devadasis, solar power systems for anganwadis without electricity, the Mazi Kanya Bhagyashree scheme, financial assistance to NGOs running shelter homes, and monetary aid for children affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.The department said the number of organisations availing benefits under the multipurpose social centres scheme had declined in recent years.Alternative arrangements, including women empowerment centres and Sakhi One Stop Centres in every district, provide information, guidance, counselling and links to relevant services.The grants scheme for women's groups was also reviewed as programmes for skill development, training, awareness and empowerment are being implemented through other agencies. The department clarified this did not mean such activities or awareness programmes for women would be discontinued.Regarding financial assistance for the rehabilitation of children of devadasis, the department said legal provisions to eradicate the devadasi practice had been in place since 2005. No expenditure was incurred under the scheme in the previous year, and no proposals for rehabilitation of such children had been received from district-level authorities, it said.The department noted the revised Lek Ladki scheme had replaced the Majhi Kanya Bhagyashree scheme, with eligible girls entitled to financial assistance at specified stages.On assistance to NGOs running shelter homes, the department said information available with it indicated only three such homes were operational.Eligible beneficiaries under the financial assistance scheme for children who were orphaned or rendered homeless during the pandemic have been included in the Savitribai Phule Child Care Scheme, said the order.Services and benefits would continue through existing mechanisms, including Mission Shakti, Shakti Sadan, Sakhi One Stop Centres, women empowerment centres, the Lek Ladki Yojana, the Savitribai Phule Child Care Scheme and Mission Vatsalya, it added.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

title: BJP supporter shot dead in Bengal, 6 injured as incident triggers clashes
description: Locals alleged that Samir Ghosh was killed by people associated with a rival political party.
content: A 35-year-old Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) supporter died after unidentified assailants attacked him in West Bengal’s Malda district on Wednesday evening, police said on Thursday. Samir Ghosh was assaulted with sharp weapons before being shot twice in the Ramkeli area, news agency PTI reported.The incident triggered clashes between two groups, leaving at least six people injured. Police said the injured received treatment at Malda Medical College and Hospital.Locals alleged that Ghosh was killed by people associated with a rival political party. Police have not confirmed the motive behind the killing.Police had not arrested anyone in connection with the case as of Thursday. They deployed a large contingent of personnel to prevent further violence. Officials said the situation remained under control, PTI reported.Earlier clashes between BJP and TMC workersThe latest incident comes about a month after a clash in the Naldubi area of Malda left five BJP workers injured.Police arrested 12 people, including TMC panchayat member Ripon Burman and members of his family, following the clash, according to a Times of India report.The confrontation reportedly stemmed from a longstanding dispute linked to a panchayat election. BJP leaders accused Burman and his supporters of attacking party workers, while Burman denied the allegations and claimed he was being framed.

title: We share same concerns as India: Marco Rubio on US-Pakistan ties and Delhi's fight against terror
description: He was responding to a question on how the US would reassure New Delhi that its closer ties with Pakistan would not weaken India's efforts to fight terrorism.
content: US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Washington's close ties with Pakistan would not affect its partnership with India, adding that both countries shared concerns over terrorism."In no way does the relationship with Pakistan come at the expense of our relationship with India," Rubio, who was on a visit to India, said in an interview with India Today. He added that the US and India "share the same concerns... about terrorism."He made the remarks at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel in Mumbai, one of the locations targeted in the 26/11 terror attacks in 2008. The attacks killed more than 160 people, including six US nationals. He was responding to a question on how Washington would reassure New Delhi that its closer ties with Islamabad would not weaken India's efforts to fight terrorism.Rubio on US-Pakistan ties and IndiaHe said the US had global interests that required it to maintain ties with countries across the world, including Pakistan, with which it has had longstanding relations.Rubio added that closer engagement could give Washington greater scope to influence Islamabad's decisions on several issues. "I think it allows us to have, hopefully, more influence over the decisions they make on a variety of topics," he said.While speaking about the US record on counterterrorism, Rubio said his country had also suffered from terrorist attacks and remained committed to tackling the threat worldwide."No country in the world does more to go after terrorism than the United States," he said, referring to US operations that dismantled the Islamic State's territorial stronghold, weakened Al-Qaeda and killed its founder, Osama bin Laden.Marco Rubio in IndiaDuring his India visit, Rubio also sought to address concerns about Washington's stricter immigration rules. He said the changes were part of a broader effort to reform the US immigration system and were not specifically aimed at India.He held talks with external affairs minister S Jaishankar, with discussions largely covering trade, energy, defence, technology and people-to-people ties.On Wednesday, Rubio met leaders of some of India's largest business groups. His meetings included Tata Group chairman N Chandrasekaran and Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani, before he travelled to Jamnagar for a tour with Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani.Speaking about the proposed India-US trade deal, Rubio said the two countries were “very, very close” to an agreement, with only a few details left to resolve.His remarks on India’s Russian oil purchases were also significant. He said the importance of maintaining strong ties with India was one factor behind US President Donald Trump's recent decision to waive tariffs on India and other countries over their purchases of Russian energy.Rubio also acknowledged that India would find it difficult to reduce its dependence on Russian crude oil in a short period.

title: U.S. treasury yields edge up, bond market focus to stay on France
description: Treasury yields edged higher, having slid sharply on Thursday as investors sought safe havens from the turmoil in French government bonds.
content: U.S. Treasury yields edged higher in Asian trade on Friday, having slid sharply on Thursday as investors sought safe havens from the turmoil in French government bonds.The 10-year Treasury yield, which fell below 5% for the first time in a month on Thursday, traded 1.5 basis points higher at 4.967%, according to Tradeweb. The 10-year Treasury yield declined 19.3 basis points on Thursday in its largest one-day fall since March 2023.Investors’ concern over France’s fiscal challenges and the risk that high oil prices could dent economic growth have prompted a search for safe haven investments, and U.S. Treasurys were beneficiaries of that.“The market has real concerns about the French fiscal situation,” said Maria Llerena, director of financial research at Domini Impact Investments.Protests, a government trying to pass a budget and presidential elections in the spring of 2027 “complicate things further.”Sharp selloffs pushed the 10-year French OAT yield to 5.142% on Thursday, the highest level since 2002, while the 10-year OAT-Bund yield spread widened to 177 basis points, the widest since late 2011, according to LSEG.On Friday, Moody’s Ratings will review France. The ratings firm has an Aa3 rating with negative outlook on France, “and there is a significant likelihood of a downgrade,” said Jens Naervig Pedersen, director in fixed income and forex research at Danske Bank, in a note.A downgrade, however, is fully priced in and it should not have a significant impact, he said, shifting the focus on the outlook of the rating.“If Moody’s places France on a stable outlook, then the focus on the rating should diminish,” he said.Write to Emese Bartha at emese.bartha@wsj.com

title: Former Israeli military chief, ex-PM: Benjamin Netanyahu’s top rivals in the Israeli elections
description: While Israel votes for parties and not candidates, there are some prominent figures who have emerged as front-runners for the prime ministerial post.
content: As Israel heads to vote on October 27, a host of political figures, including an ex-prime minister and a former military chief, have positioned themselves as challengers seeking to replace Benjamin Netanyahu. While Israel votes for parties and not single candidates to enter the 120-seat Knesset, there are some prominent figures who have emerged as front-runners for the prime ministerial post.The key faces include Prime Minister Netanyahu from the Likud Party; former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot from Yashar; Israel’s minister of national security Itamar Ben-Gvir of Otzma Yehudit; Bezalel Smotrich of the Religious Zionist Party; and former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who announced a joint ticket in April, later named B'Yachad.Yair Golan from The Democrats, and Avigdor Lieberman from Yisrael Beiteunu are also in contention.The contest is one of the most significant ones, given that it is the first in four years and also the first since the October 2023 Hamas-led attack, following which Israel declared a war on Gaza that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians till now, according to Gaza’s health ministry. The contenders have alleged security failures leading to the October 2023 attack, and criticised Netanyahu’s handling of the wars with Gaza and Iran as well as West Bank settler violence.Also Read | JD Vance sidesteps Netanyahu's endorsement ahead of Israel elections, says Trump's backing ‘most influential’But first, how does Israel vote?The current electoral threshold in Israel is 3.25 per cent, meaning a political party must receive at least 3.25 per cent of the votes in order to gain a seat in the Knesset. The majority mark is 61 of the 120 seats, and no party has ever won this outright, meaning that all governments have relied on coalitions.Seat-sharing is on a proportional basis. Each party gets seats in proportion to their share in the national vote. For example, a party winning 30 per cent of the votes will get approximately 30 per cent of the seats. Meanwhile, the votes for parties which fail to secure 3.25 per cent of the votes are discarded.Netanyahu's rival contendersHere’s what we know about the candidates seeking to replace Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving premier, and their parties, along with the key issues they are fighting on.Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar)Known as Netanyahu’s biggest rival, Gadi Eisenkot, 66, is the chairman of Yashar (‘honest’ in Hebrew), a party he founded only last year.Military and political experience: Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israeli military. Born in Tiberias in 1960 to a traditional family and then raised in Eilat, he enlisted in the Golani Brigade in 1978, where he served as a rifleman in Battalion 13 up to brigade commander. According to his party’s website, Eisenkot served 41 years in the IDF and held a series of key positions, including serving as military secretary to two PMs, being commander of the Judea and Samaria Division during the Second Intifada, as head of the operations directorate, as commander of the commander of Northern Command and finally as the deputy chief of staff.He became the IDF's 21st chief of staff in 2015. While in the IDF, he advanced the multi-year "Gideon" plan to improve the IDF's capabilities on land, in the air and sea. He was first elected to the Knesset in 2022, and served as a minister in the War Cabinet following the October 7, 2023 attack.Key issues: Eisenkot is a self-styled moderate, and has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu’s approach on aspects of the Gaza war. He is also a military realist, insisting two years ago that Israel was unlikely to win “total victory” over Hamas, and calling for a strategy which prioritised the lives of hostages, The Guardian reported. His son, Gal, and two of his nephews were killed in the Gaza conflict.Eisenkot has opposed the two-state solution, calling it “delusional” following the October 7, 2023 attack, Times of Israel reported.In the lead-up to the polls, he has maintained that his allies would need to agree that Israel is a Jewish and democratic state, that military service is universal and that Hamas is a terrorist organisation which must be dismantled.Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid (B'Yachad )Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett (2021-22) and Yair Lapid (July-December 2022) announced a joint ticket in April this year, which was later named B'Yachad (“Together”). Bennett, 54, is poised to be prime minister if the party wins.Bennett, Lapid’s political career: Bennett’s political career began with the leader he is now seeking to replace, with him serving as Netanyahu’s chief of staff from 2006 to 2008. Netanyahu was then in the opposition. Bennett and Netanyahu won the Bayit Yehudi leadership in 2012, following which they held a coalition agreement that neither would join without the other. Bennett joined the Netanyahu-led coalition following the 2015 election, holding the post of education minister. He was appointed defence minister in 2019. However, he was out of Netanyahu’s government in 2020, and became the leader of a coalition government with Yair Lapid in 2021.Yair Lapid, 62, formed the Yesh Atid in 2012 after a career in journalism, with the party positioning itself as a secular, centrist, liberal-Zionist force. It focused on the concerns of working Israelis, the economic burden on the middle class, and greater equality in military service, according to The Jerusalem Post.In its first election in 2013, Lapid’s party won 19 seats and became Knesset’s second-largest party. Lapid also became finance minister in Netanyahu’s government. In the present Knesset too, Yesh Atid is the second-largest party, holding 24 seats, and Lapid serves as opposition leader. Lapid had served as the foreign minister and alternate prime minister in the government he formed with Bennett in 2021, which was dissolved in 2022.Also Read | Netanyahu warns future US president could be hostile to Israel, eyes close ties with IndiaPolitical stance and key issues: The party combines Bennett’s right-wing political background with Lapid’s centrist Yesh Atid party, according to The Jerusalem Post. Therefore, the party and its candidates offer an amalgamation of a right-wing security stance along with liberal positions on issues of religion and state. The party is contesting majorly on concerns around cost-of-living and Israel’s education system, thus putting forward a reforms-first approach.Itamar Ben-Gvir (Otzma Yehudit)Itamar Ben-Gvir leads the Otzma Yehudit, which was once shunned as too extreme for mainstream politics, and has also pulled Netanyahu’s government further to the right since 2022, JNS reported.Political career and sanctions: A lawyer by profession, the 50-year-old has served as the minister of national security since 2022, except for a two-month gap in 2025. He first became a Knesset member in 2021, when his party unexpectedly won seven seats. Gvir, who has been accused of supporting terrorism and has criminal convictions for incitement to racism, has been sanctioned in the UK, France and others for backing the Gaza war. Key issues: Otzma Yehudit advocates the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians from Gaza, with its rallies also drawing extremist chants. In government, it has sponsored judicial reforms and the death penalty for Palestinians, and its junior ministers have discussed nuking Gaza, according to Middle East Eye.The party has campaigned on issues like personal security, Jewish sovereignty and tougher measures against terrorism. This will be the party’s first time running independently since it entered the Knesset.Gvir’s tense relations with Netanyahu: Gvir recently said he wants to form a government without Netanyahu, a culmination to tense relations between the two leaders for the past two decades.Gvir earlier this month claimed Netanyahu had promised European officials that he would keep his far-right Otzma Yehudit party out of his coalition if he wins reelection next week. At a press conference in Jerusalem, Ben Gvir said he had “received information about messages” from Netanyahu’s office making such a pledge, Times of Israel reported.Bezalel Smotrich (Religious Zionist Party)Religious Zionist Party (RZP) leader Bezalel Smotrich is currently finance minister in the Netanyahu-led Israeli government. He has overseen massive state spending on settlement initiatives, the Associated Press reported.Key issues: Smotrich’s party supports an aggressive security policy, increasing settlements and solidifying Israeli control over the occupied West Bank. The party joined with farther-right Zehut (Identity) but is struggling to pass the threshold.Also Read | Arab voters could hold key to Netanyahu's future in Israel election In 2022, it had a strong showing amid an electoral pact with Otzma Yehudit. However, both parties have now severed ties with Netanyahu’s Likud Party to run as competitors, despite the Israeli PM’s proposal for alliance.RZP backs military conscription for ultra-Orthodox communities, but has voted for Haredi-backed laws, such as stopping arrests of Haredi draft dodgers, while sitting alongside Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition government.Support base: 46-year-old Smotrich, the son of an Orthodox rabbi, draws support from a more religious base than Ben Gvir, according to Middle East Eye. He has sought the implementation of Jewish law (halacha), and says Torah scripture has underpinned his strategy as finance minister since 2022.He also demands a judicial overhaul, the abolition of the Oslo Accords, the dismantlement of the Palestinian Authority, and the Israeli settlement of Gaza and the West Bank, while calling himself a “proud homophobe”.Yair Golan (The Democrats)Yair Golan is the leader of the Democrats, the party created through the unification of the two historic left-wing parties Labor and Meretz. In Israel's present political scenario, his is the only party which offers an explicitly Zionist, liberal and social-democratic alternative, The Jewish Chronicle reported.While this creates a separate identity for Golan, it also limits electoral appeal in a country which has moved sharply to the right in the past three years, particularly following the October, 2023 attack. Personal life and political career: Golan, 64, was born in Rishon LeZion in 1962, and served in the IDF for nearly four decades. He joined the Paratroopers Brigade in the Israeli military, and rose up the ranks to command the Nahal Brigade, the Judea and Samaria Division, the Home Front Command and the Northern Command. Golan was eventually appointed chief of staff and was even in line to lead the IDF. His military career establishes him as a serious security figure, The Jewish Chronicle reported.Golan entered politics in 2019 through an alliance led by former PM Ehud Barak and later joined Meretz. However, in 2022, Meretz failed to cross the electoral threshold. He was catapulted to prominence following the October, 2023 attack, when the retired general drove independently into communities near Gaza and located and rescued survivors of Nova music festival. The festival was one of the sites targeted by Hamas. He then won the Labor leadership with 95 per cent of the vote in May, 2024, and united Labor with Meretz to form the Democrats party.Political stance on key issues: The Democrats party balances strong security posture along with support for renewed diplomacy. It calls for protection of judicial independence, civil equality, greater investment in public services and universal military or national service.Golan has personally argued for Israel to remain militarily adept while also seeking a framework which prevents permanent rule over Palestinians. This places him to the left of other major opposition parties.While Golan is not running for prime minister specifically, his party has signalled willingness to join any coalition replacing Netanyahu. Golan has also seemed open to cooperate politically with Arab parties and has campaigned in Arab communities, according to The Jewish Chronicle.Avigdor Lieberman (Yisrael Beiteinu)Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and a former minister, is an emigre from Soviet-era eastern Europe.. The 58-year-old's party, founded in 1998, is right-wing and relies on Israel’s 1.5 million Russian speakers for support, according to Middle East Eye.While the party has at its best become the third largest in elections, it has still been in coalition with seven of the last 10 governments in Israel. However, Lieberman has this time announced that he will not join or support a minority government. He has also ruled out sitting with Arab-majority parties or any other faction he considers non-Zionist, Times of Israel reported.Political career: Lieberman served as director-general of the Likud movement from 1993 to 1996. He was pivotal in turning Netanyahu, then a newly elected party leader, into Likud’s dominant figure. Netanyahu appointed Lieberman director-general of the Prime Minister's office after becoming the prime minister in 1996.However, three years later, Lieberman broke away to establish Yisrael Beiteinu. However, he has had close ties with Likud, even running on a joint ticket with Netanyahu in 2013.Key issues and poll strategy: Liberman is a hardline right-winger and a resident of the West Bank settlement of Nokdim. His views on security and Palestine almost align with those of the far-right ministers, including Ben Gvir and Smotrich. Lieberman has said that he plans to lure right-wing Knesset members away from Likud to reach the threshold to enter Knesset, claiming he knows several MPs from Netanyahu's party who feel the Israeli PM has made them subservient to the ultra-Orthodox parties, according to Times of Israel.He has also claimed to have support from first-time young voters, who he says will support the change bloc over the ruling coalition.

title: US State Department rejects report of foreign service officers' loyalty to Trump being tested before promotion
description: Allegations that diplomats were screened for political views have intensified scrutiny of State Department staffing changes under Marco Rubio.
content: The US State Department has reportedly questioned some career diplomats seeking senior assignments about their voting history in the past three presidential elections, raising concerns over alleged political bias in federal government hiring and promotions under President Donald Trump’s administration.According to The Washington Sun, candidates who voted for Trump were eligible for mid- to upper-level Foreign Service positions, while campaign donations were also scrutinized. The report has drawn criticism from lawmakers and former diplomats, who argue that professional experience, rather than political loyalty, should determine appointments to senior diplomatic roles.A State Department spokesperson rejected the allegation, calling the suggestion that officials were asked about their political affiliations for promotions an “absurd premise”.The spokesperson told The Hill on Thursday that the administration would prioritize merit over the number of years employees had served at the department. Questions about “fidelity”, the spokesperson said, concerned upholding the Constitution, following the law and implementing policies in the interests of the American people.Also Read: Raja Krishnamoorthi warns of rising anti-Indian hate on social media, calls for Big Tech accountability“It is not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the President’s vision for foreign policy,” the spokesperson said.Foreign Service association considers legal optionsThe American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), the professional association and union representing Foreign Service officers, said it had heard accounts of senior career officials being denied positions after interviews that included politically oriented questions.The association said such questioning had no place in federal service and was exploring possible legal options.Federal law prohibits discrimination against federal employees based on political affiliation. Career Foreign Service and civil service officers are also required to perform their duties in a neutral and nonpartisan manner, although the executive branch can appoint political officials to designated positions.Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the outgoing ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said lawmakers had been examining whether political affiliation was becoming a factor in federal employment.Also Read: US visa bulletin November 2026: Latest update brings selective progress for Indian green card applicants“These are critical national security positions and individuals should be chosen for their experience and ability, not their political loyalty,” Shaheen told The Washington Sun, adding that lawmakers were working to investigate the allegations.Rep. James Walkinshaw, a Democrat from Virginia, also criticized the reported practice, saying on X that basing civil service decisions on political affiliations or donations was illegal.Rubio’s restructuring draws further scrutinyThe allegations come amid wider changes at the State Department under Secretary of State Marco Rubio. In July 2025, the department added a “fidelity” component to employee evaluation criteria, assessing how officials protect and promote executive power, Federal News Network reported at the time. The assessment reportedly linked to a White House webpage listing Trump’s executive orders and presidential actions.Earlier in 2026, Rubio laid off approximately 1,100 civil service employees and 250 Foreign Service officers as part of a restructuring effort. The department said the cuts followed the elimination of specific bureaus and offices, while critics argued that experienced staff were unfairly affected.The State Department maintains that its approach focuses on merit and policy implementation. The reported allegations have yet to be established as unlawful political discrimination.

title: Tom Tiffany campaign staffer Eric Brooks cited for first-offense OWI ahead of tough Wisconsin gubernatorial race
description: Eric Brooks, who also serves on the Waukesha School Board, was arrested in Eau Claire and cited for driving while intoxicated.
content: A staff member for Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany’s campaign has been cited for first-offense operating while intoxicated (OWI) in Wisconsin, according to Eau Claire County court records reviewed by local news outlet The Recombobulation Area.Eric Brooks, who also holds an elected seat on the Waukesha School Board, was arrested on October 16 and formally cited on October 19, court records show. He also received a citation for driving a vehicle without required lamps lighted, with both alleged violations stemming from the October 16 incident.Tiffany, a Republican congressman representing Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District, launched his gubernatorial campaign earlier this year. His campaign has focused on education, taxes, border security and public safety.Neither Brooks nor Tiffany’s campaign immediately issued a public statement addressing the citations.Also read: Gaffes, scepticism and divide: A look at Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for Ohio governorCourt records outline allegationsAccording to The Recombobulation Area, Brooks was booked following the Oct. 16 incident in Eau Claire County, western Wisconsin.The records identify one count of Operating While Intoxicated: First Offense and another for operation without required lamps lighted.According to Wisconsin OWI Laws, a first-offence OWI is typically punishable by fines, licence revocation and mandatory alcohol assessment. It is generally not treated as a criminal offense unless additional circumstances apply, such as injury, repeat offenses or a minor passenger in the vehicle.As of publication, no additional court filings alleging more serious offenses had been reported.Also read: Kristi Noem's former aide Corey Lewandowski facing DOJ probe over alleged misconduct at DHS: ReportsBrooks recently drew attention over campaign eventBrooks was recently in the spotlight during Tom Tiffany’s gubernatorial campaign after he barred reporters from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel from attending a campaign event in Milwaukee on September 24.The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel shared the video of the incident on social media which showed Brooks stopping the journalists from entering the event claiming that the publication is not “covering the race fairly.” Brooks serves as an elected member of the Waukesha School Board, one of Wisconsin’s largest school districts. He has also been active in Republican political organizing in the state.Local media reported that because of the OWI offense, Brooks is now being urged by a Waukesha parent organization to “immediately step down from the Waukesha School Board.”

title: Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, blasts ‘outrageous’ report on alleged undisclosed foreign bank accounts
description: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, criticized a report allegedly revealing his secret financial agreements with Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.
content: President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, heavily criticized a report which allegedly revealed his secret financial agreements with Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.Kushner's remarks came on Thursday after Vanity Fair published an excerpt from an upcoming book.What Jared Kushner said about the reportKushner wrote on X "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them. No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations.During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.Also Read | Trump calls for Ilhan Omar's resignation as Minnesota congresswoman's ‘real name’ is questioned amid federal investigationThese are outrageous fabrications being presented as investigative journalism. This is not journalism. It is a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent." What are the allegations against Jared KushnerAs per the article, the allegations against Kushner involve secret bank accounts, where he was a signatory. It also includes hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign transfers and political arrangements with leaders in the Middle East.The report noted that Dutch investigators came across these findings after gaining access to Kushner’s phone through a Russian hacker who had been apprehended and flipped.The phone use from 2018 was monitored by said Dutch investigators, who reportedly found Trump's son-in-law access a bank account linked to the UAE, that had $750 million transferred into it by a charity funded by the UAE government. An unnamed person also reportedly held discussions with officials from Israel and the UAE about a ‘secret financial agreement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia.’The Vanity Fair report cited this person and noted that they alleged Kushner promised UAE president Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan that he would ‘push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund.’ Trump's son-in-law appeared to take exception to the excerpt from the story which suggested that he might have violated US law by allegedly failing to disclose his activity with the account in question. The report went on to allege that Al Nahyan used another bank account meant for Kushner and moved $1 billion to Israel via Azerbaijan for Kushner. The report also claimed that presidents of the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were paying for Kushner's influence in the US government. This is the latest allegation Kushner is facing, after Rep. Robert Garcia of California opened a House Oversight Committee investigation into Ivanka Trump's husband. This came following a CNN report which alleged Kushner's private equity firm became the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial, which invests in companies providing Israel with military equipment. Kushner, who's part of the Israel-Gaza peace efforts, rejected the CNN report and alleged the publication was suggesting his work in the Middle East ‘somehow benefited investments in Israeli defense companies.’

title: 'May go a little further': Trump warns of escalation in West Asia war; Iran threatens wider retaliation
description: The US-Iran war, which began in late February, has led to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and heightened tensions across West Asia
content: US President Donald Trump has warned of a further escalation in the war with Iran, saying he may “go a little further” to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon.Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Trump said the US had “knocked the hell out of Iran” and argued that previous presidents should have taken similar action.“I'm doing what should have been done by other presidents. We can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon. In one way, people probably don't love it, but many people — many great patriots — really do. This should have been done a long time ago by other presidents. We've knocked the hell out of them, and we may go a little further,” he said. Also Read | ‘Not negotiating’: Trump says 'something will happen fairly soon' with Iran, as US mulls fresh strikesIn another video, speaking at a campaign rally at Sioux Gateway Airport in Sioux City, Iowa, Trump said the conflict with Iran would end soon, adding that the outcome would bring down fuel prices.“We're gonna have Iran finished very soon. One way or the other. It's almost insignificant to me which way,” he said. “It's going to be done very soon, and your gasoline prices and your oil is going to come tumbling down.”The war with Iran, which began in late February, has led to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and heightened tensions across West Asia, with ships coming under attack and civilians also being killed.Tehran warns of wider attacks on civilian targets: ReportMeanwhile, Iran has warned that if the US and Israel resume strikes on its territory, it will retaliate by targeting not only American military bases but also airports, pipelines and other civilian infrastructure in neighbouring West Asian countries, The Wall Street Journal reported.Also Read | Mojtaba warned this would happen? Iran threatens US bases after blasting 7 ships, Hormuz in chaosIn the first phase of the war, Iran inflicted significant damage on US air bases, embassies and the headquarters of the US 5th Fleet in Bahrain. It also struck energy and industrial facilities in the United Arab Emirates, a major gas plant in Qatar, and airports in Dubai, Kuwait and Bahrain.Tehran has warned that it would seek to inflict greater damage in any renewed round of fighting, at a time when stocks of air-defence interceptors needed by the US and Arab militaries to repel attacks have been running low, says WSJ report. Israel's interceptor supplies have also come under pressure.Also Read | Iran claims it struck 4 oil ships in Persian Gulf, 3 others hit mines in Strait of HormuzIran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in an opinion piece in the Financial Times that renewed attacks “will put civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk”.Analysts estimate that Iran has hundreds to thousands of ballistic missiles, while US and regional officials believe Tehran has resumed limited production using stockpiled components and underground facilities.These developments come as efforts to secure a peace deal remain deadlocked and the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked.

title: In 2025, Japan’s environment ministry showcased Fukushima cleanup soil reused in managed public works, with final disposal outside due by 2045
description: Japan is using some low-radioactivity soil from the Fukushima cleanup in public works to reduce waste needing disposal by 2045.
content: For years, huge quantities of soil dug up during the cleanup of Fukushima have been stored in vast facilities near the site of the 2011 nuclear disaster. Now, Japan is trying something unusual with some of it: putting the soil back into public infrastructure under strict controls.Japan is giving some of the soil removed during the Fukushima nuclear cleanup a second life by using it in carefully controlled public works instead of sending all of it to permanent disposal. Japan’s Ministry of the Environment states that final disposal of removed soil and other waste generated by the cleanup must be completed outside Fukushima by March 2045. Rather than sending all of the material to a permanent disposal site, the government plans to reduce the amount requiring disposal by recycling soil with low levels of radioactive contamination in carefully managed public works.Why is Fukushima soil still being stored?The soil was removed during extensive decontamination work following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant accident. Workers scraped contaminated topsoil from residential areas, farmland and other locations and transported it to an Interim Storage Facility covering about 1,600 hectares in the towns of Okuma and Futaba. By the end of March 2025, about 14.08 million cubic meters of removed soil and waste had been transported to the facility.The storage site was intended to be temporary; however, the government later set a deadline for final disposal. Under Japanese law, the government must take the necessary measures to complete final disposal outside Fukushima within 30 years of the start of transportation to the facility, putting the deadline at March 2045. That creates a difficult problem: moving millions of cubic meters of material elsewhere would require a large disposal site, while keeping everything in Fukushima would conflict with the promise that the material would eventually leave the prefecture. The government therefore began investigating whether some of the less-contaminated soil could instead become a construction material.How can contaminated soil be reused?The approach is known as managed recycling. It does not mean simply taking contaminated earth and spreading it around. Soil must first meet specified radioactivity standards and then be used in projects where its movement, exposure, and long-term condition can be controlled. In March 2025, Japan's Environment Ministry established formal standards for managed recycling. Recycled material made from removed soil must contain radioactive cesium at 8,000 becquerels per kilogram or less, a level the ministry says corresponds to an additional effective dose of no more than 1 millisievert per year under the relevant exposure scenario.In addition, there should be a mechanism to prevent the material from dispersing or washing away. Radiation dose monitoring must take place during construction, operation, and maintenance of the facilities, along with the documentation of the location, amount, and radioactivity of the recycled soil. The Environment Ministry has required covering in some cases, with the recycled soil placed beneath a layer of uncontaminated material to limit environmental exposure. The government had already tested the approach before setting these standards. Some demonstration projects were carried out in Fukushima; among them were an agricultural land project in the Nagadoro area of Iitate Village and a road embankment project in the Interim Storage Facility. What happens to the rest by 2045?The organization is also researching technologies that can help separate and process the extracted materials in such a way that more volume of low-radioactivity soil could possibly be recycled while keeping the radioactive soil at a minimum volume that needs to be disposed of. Among the technologies being researched are soil sorting and heat treatment.The strategy requires balancing safety, waste management, and public acceptance. Despite such soil passing all required tests, Japanese society in other parts of the country might have a problem accepting soil contaminated with radioactive materials linked to the Fukushima disaster. The authorities have treated public awareness as a separate part of the strategy alongside recycling and disposal. The interim facility stores soil collected during the world's largest nuclear decontamination effort.It is an attempt to turn part of a long-term waste problem into a controlled resource while reducing the burden of final disposal. Whether the approach can be expanded beyond demonstration projects, gain broad public acceptance, and ultimately help meet the 2045 deadline remains one of the most consequential questions in Fukushima's continuing recovery.

title: After the 2004 tsunami emptied India’s Trinket Island, abandoned cattle went feral; a 2020 study reported that only about 150 descendants remained
description: After the 2004 tsunami emptied Trinket Island, its cattle were left to survive without human care. Researchers reported about 150 descendants in 2020.
content: For generations, cattle on Trinket Island were part of human life in India's Nicobar archipelago. Then, on Dec. 26, 2004, a massive earthquake and tsunami struck the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, devastating Trinket and forcing its human population to leave. The cattle were left behind.The cattle's story took an unexpected turn, as the animals were left to survive on their own after the tsunami. Once cared for by people, they became completely feral, adapting to life on the isolated island. By 2020, researchers reported that only about 150 descendants remained, leaving the herd highly vulnerable to extinction.From Danish livestock to island cattleThe story of Trinket's cattle began more than two centuries before the tsunami. The 2020 Journal of Genetics paper, citing a 1903 account by Kloss, said Danish colonists introduced cattle to the island between 1756 and 1768 apparently to provide milk. The animals were initially managed by the colonial settlers, but that arrangement changed after Danish control ended. The indigenous Nicobarese subsequently cared for the herd but primarily valued cattle for meat rather than milk. Over time, the animals became semi-feral. The report said researchers noted nearly 50 semi-wild cows on Trinket Island in the early 20th century. These cows also helped transform the island’s landscape. The researchers stated that part of the forest on Trinket Island was transformed into grassland by the Danes, which would act as fodder for the cows. Therefore, this historical context shows the herd was more than simply cattle left behind after the tsunami.What happened after the tsunami?The 2004 disaster changed the cattle's relationship with people almost overnight. Trinket was among the islands severely affected by the tsunami, and the surviving inhabitants were evacuated to neighboring islands. With no human community left to manage the animals, the cattle became completely feral. Unlike conventional cattle, the animals no longer depended on people for regular feeding, breeding management, or veterinary care. They had to find food and shelter themselves, while living within the limits of a small island environment.The population's precarious condition was documented in The Indian Journal of Animal Sciences. Researchers examined blood-based indicators including hematological values, serum biochemistry, and mineral profiles. The measurements fell within normal physiological ranges and provided baseline data for future health assessments. The same paper reported that only around 150 descendants were then known to exist. That number placed the cattle close to the edge of extinction and highlighted the need for conservation measures. What does their DNA reveal?The cattle's unusual history also prompted researchers to investigate where they came from genetically. Scientists also examined mitochondrial DNA, focusing on the D-loop and cytochrome b regions. The analysis placed Trinket cattle within the Bos indicus lineage and identified them as the I2 sub-haplotype. Researchers suggested that this genetic signature may reflect the historical movement of the I2 lineage toward Southeast Asia. The finding offered a way to distinguish the isolated island population from other cattle and provided information that could be useful for conservation breeding.The Trinket cattle also carry the legacy of a colonial experiment that outlasted its original purpose. Their history reflects shifting human dynamics, transitioning from colonial livestock management to indigenous husbandry to total post-tsunami abandonment. The existence of just about 150 of these animals, as recorded in the 2020 study, is indicative of the rapid rate at which such unique genetic inheritance can be lost.

title: In 1959, two men released 12 snowshoe hares on a Canadian island; the animals spread, hindered tree growth, and were eradicated in 2007
description: Introduced to Hay Island in 1959 by two fishermen, snowshoe hares multiplied and spread to Kent Island.
content: In 1959, two New Brunswick fishermen came up with a simple plan for 12 snowshoe hares. Wesley Ingalls and his nephew, Junior, carried the animals by boat from Grand Manan Island to nearby Hay Island in the Bay of Fundy. They hoped the hares would reproduce and give them something to trap during the winter, when they were not fishing.Instead, the experiment transformed the islands' forests. The hares multiplied rapidly and crossed from Hay Island to neighboring Kent Island. Research published in The Canadian Field-Naturalist found that tree recruitment on Kent Island plummeted after the 1959 introduction and remained low, while trees continued to establish on nearby hare-free Outer Wood Island. It took repeated attempts and nearly half a century before the last hare was trapped in 2007.How 12 hares became a forest problemSnowshoe hares were native to mainland New Brunswick, but they had not naturally established themselves on the small islands where Ingalls released them. The absence of competing mammals and the limited ability of local predators to catch them in dense vegetation gave the newcomers an advantage. The hares reproduced quickly. A female could produce several litters a year, and the population grew from the original dozen to hundreds. At low tide, the animals could cross the exposed land between Hay and Kent islands. Soon, the problem was no longer confined to the place where the fishermen had released them. The effects became visible in the island’s plant life. The young saplings of the balsam fir and other trees were continually being grazed upon before they could grow and become the next generation of trees in the forest. In 1961, Junior returned to Hay Island to cut the young balsam firs to build a herring weir and found that the stand of trees was no longer able to regenerate like it used to. Researchers eventually compared tree growth on Kent Island with that on hare-free Outer Wood Island.Why the trees could not grow backThe damage was more than a matter of hungry animals eating a few saplings. The hares became a powerful force shaping the ecosystem. They browsed the growing tips of young white spruce, sometimes reaching branches high above the ground. In some areas, their droppings reached densities of about 50 per square meter. When researchers enclosed small plots so hares could not enter, seedling densities inside the protected areas eventually exceeded 150 per square meter, compared with none outside the fences. These observations, documented by Wheelwright in Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment, showed how strongly the introduced hares were suppressing forest regeneration.The difference helped rule out other possible explanations for the lack of forest regeneration, including the harsh climate and the Bay of Fundy's salty fog. The hares kept young trees from surviving long enough to replace aging canopy trees. By the 1980s, storms were increasingly knocking down older trees, while few young trees were available to replace them. Forested areas began turning into open tangles dominated by plants such as wood fern and raspberry. Removing the animal that changed the islandRemoving the hares proved much more difficult than introducing them. In 1998, Nathaniel Wheelwright, an ecologist at Bowdoin College, initiated a trapping experiment with the approval of the government of New Brunswick. The trapping reduced the hare population, but it recovered within two years. Again in 2002, the same thing happened. Hares were very difficult to catch; they bred rapidly and could live in the thick vegetation of the island. Wheelwright finally consulted with the vertebrate pest control officials of New Zealand, who told him that it could be done.However, the final campaign was successful. In 2007, the last snowshoe hare was caught following almost 50 years on the islands. The ecological reaction to this was rather rapid. Without browsing pressure, seedlings and saplings were able to start growing across the forest floor because they were no longer being eaten.

title: A 2026 study sequenced 30 feral Hong Kong cattle, finding genetic clues to their ancestry and possible adaptations
description: A genome study of 30 Hong Kong feral cattle found high genetic diversity alongside signs of inbreeding.
content: Cattle once served as working animals for farmers in Hong Kong, but changing economic conditions eventually led to the decline of cattle farming. Then, in the 1970s, some cattle were abandoned and began roaming freely. Generations later, the animals have become a distinctive feral population, living with little of the human management that shaped domestic cattle.Now, their DNA is offering clues to what happened after that change. A 2026 genome study sequenced 30 Hong Kong feral cattle and compared them with 116 cattle from four major populations. The results revealed a population that retained surprisingly high genetic diversity despite its small size, while also carrying genetic signatures linked to its long history of isolation, ancient wild-bovine ancestry and adaptation to the local environment.When cattle stopped living by human rulesThe Hong Kong cattle population is thought to number about 1,000 animals. Researchers collected samples mainly from Sai Kung, Lantau Island, and the eastern and northern New Territories. Unlike conventional livestock, these animals have faced environmental pressures without the same level of protection, controlled breeding, and veterinary care normally provided to farm cattle. That makes the population unusually valuable for studying what happens when domesticated animals become feral. A 2020 study had already found that Hong Kong cattle were genetically distinctive and showed evidence of ancestry connected with wild bovines. That earlier work examined 21 Hong Kong cattle alongside 703 animals representing 36 cattle populations and wild species including gaur and banteng. In the new research, the analysis was more extensive because it examined each animal’s full genome rather than focusing mainly on selected genetic markers. The team sequenced the genomes of the 30 animals at 30x coverage depth.What does the cattle DNA reveal?Genome-wide analysis revealed that Hong Kong cattle were most closely related to East Asian indicine cattle, although the population has developed a genetic signature unique to itself. Scientists also found that the cattle's ancestors received some genetic input from banteng and gaur before diverging from other East Asian indicine cattle.Even more interesting is when this happened. It appears that the banteng introgression took place approximately 8,900 years ago, while gaur introgression occurred about 9,900 years ago. In other words, some of the genes in today’s feral cattle may have entered the lineage long before the animals became independent in Hong Kong.The cattle showed an unusual combination of high genetic diversity and inbreeding. Despite having decreased effective population size, the cattle still maintained high genomic variation. On top of that, these cattle displayed longer segments of the same DNA sequence than several other indicine populations. How did life in the wild shape them?The investigators then looked for evidence of natural selection by testing whether certain genome regions were favored during adaptation to the cattle’s environment. Some genomic regions showed associations with traits relevant to survival, such as heat resistance, bone density, and coat pigmentation. A specific genomic region for the ADRA1A gene showed an association with heat stress response. Other genomic regions showed associations with biological functions related to development, immunity, and metabolism.The cattle’s physical appearance is another clue. The feral cattle in Hong Kong come in displaying varied fur patterns, distinct horn shapes, asymmetrical humps, and irregular body profiles. The research team found copy-number variation in genes such as NINL, DEXI, and CIITA that may help explain differences in coat color. However, the results of the research do not mean that all genetic differences have been confirmed as adaptations. The researchers listed a few of these gene regions as candidates whose effects still need to be tested.In 2026, the DNA results tell a broader story about how generations of ancestry, isolation, and natural selection shaped the population. The herd offers a rare example of how domesticated animals evolve when human influence fades. For scientists, the herd is much more than an interesting subject of genetic research. The herd’s wild-bovine ancestry, high genetic diversity, and apparent adaptation could help scientists study how heat, disease, and other pressures shape cattle evolution. For Hong Kong, the wandering herd is a living reminder of the territory’s agricultural history.

title: Indian-origin man in US claims ICE 'kidnapped' wife, arrested for murder after burnt remains found
description: The accused has been identified as 28-year-old Gurinder Gill, while the victim was his wife, 30-year-old Jasmine Gill.
content: An Indian-origin man was arrested for murdering his wife after initially alleging that she had been kidnapped by the United States' immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) agents in California.The accused has been identified as 28-year-old Gurinder Gill, while the victim was 30-year-old Jasmine Gill, according to the Sacramento County Sheriff’s statement.Jasmine was last spotted at her home in Sacramento on September 30. Four days later, on October 4, 2026, her cousin alerted authorities to her disappearance by filling a missing person report.As an investigation began into the case, Gurinder alleged that ICE officers had taken his wife away while she was collecting mail outside their home.However, inquiries with the immigration agency showed no evidence to support Gurinder’s account, as ICE informed detectives that its officers had not carried out any enforcement actions at the address, the statement said.ALSO READ: Indian-origin man starts fundraiser after daughter is allegedly murdered by her motherA detailed inquiry by the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office highlighted discrepancies in Gurinder’s account of what had happened to Jasmine. Investigators also discovered that the couple had been involved in a divorce proceeding and a dispute over child custody, a statement on October 16 detailed.Burnt remains discovered on October 1Investigators found burnt human remains in El Dorado County on October 1, later confirming that those belonged to Jasmine Gill. Based on their investigation, Homicide Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Gurinder for murder.Gurinder was taken into custody on October 14. Law enforcement officials also searched two properties linked to the accused under court-authorised warrants. He was then put into the Sacramento County Main Jail on murder charges and is ineligible for bail.ICE calls Gurinder a ‘deranged man’Reacting to the case, ICE called Gurinder a "deranged man". "These maniacs will attempt to scapegoat the brave men and women of ICE, who work around the clock to remove dangerous criminals, meanwhile they themselves commit criminal acts," ICE posted on X.ALSO READ: Indian-origin man lures estranged wife to Chicago; stabs her to death after she rejects reconciliationJasmine was raised by a single parentA GoFundMe page set up to bring Jasmine’s body back to India stated that she grew up without her father, who died when she was young. Her mother, Sukhwinder Kaur, a nurse in India, took responsibility for raising Jasmine and her brother as a single parent."There are no words to describe the heartbreak of losing Jasmine in such a devastating and unimaginable way. At just 30 years old, she had so much life left to live," her family members said on a GoFundMe page."Perhaps the most heartbreaking part of her story is that she was fighting for a better future forherself and her baby. She was seeking a divorce. She was trying to find the freedom, safety, and fresh start they both deserved. Tragically, before she could build that future, Jasmine was murdered, leaving behind the very child she was fighting so hard to protect," the page further stated.

title: In 1994, Namibia’s Cheetah Conservation Fund began placing guard dogs with farmers; a later review found losses fell for most surveyed farmers
description: A 25-year study of Namibia’s guard dog program found 91% of farmers reported reduced livestock losses, while fewer reported using lethal control.
content: When cheetahs or jackals kill livestock, farmers can face additional financial strain. Such losses can also put predators at risk of being killed in retaliation. To reduce livestock losses and limit conflict between farmers and wildlife, the Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) began placing livestock guarding dogs on Namibian farms in 1994. A 2021 review covering the program’s first 25 years found that 91% of surveyed farmers reported reduced livestock losses after receiving the dogs.Led by Laurie Marker, the research team examined placements made between 1994 and 2018. During that period, 634 dogs were placed with farmers. The researchers collected survey data covering 472 dogs through 1,567 farm surveys. The approach is relevant to cheetah conservation because more than 90% of Namibia’s cheetahs live outside protected areas, according to the review, where they may come into conflict with livestock farmers.How do the dogs help protect livestock?The program uses Anatolian shepherds and Kangal dogs, breeds originating in Turkey that have long been used to guard livestock. Puppies began bonding with small livestock at about 4 weeks old and were placed on farms between 10 and 12 weeks of age, after each farm passed an approval check. Early exposure helps the dogs develop an association with the herd and remain with the animals as they mature. Survey responses showed a marked change in reported livestock losses after the dogs arrived. In the year before placement, 19% of respondents said they had lost more than 10 livestock animals, while 7% reported losses exceeding 40 animals. In the year after placement, 67% reported no livestock losses, while 2% said they had lost more than 10 animals.Reported losses attributed to jackals fell by 45% in the year after a guarding dog was placed. Losses attributed to cheetahs declined by 16%, while those attributed to caracals fell by 15%. The differences suggest that the reported benefits varied by predator species, with the largest reduction associated with jackals. Advantages and disadvantages of the programFarmers generally viewed the dogs favorably. About 93% said the dogs met their expectations, and 99% said they would recommend the program to other farmers. Respondents rated 71% of the dogs in good condition and 22% in excellent condition.Reported use of lethal predator control also declined after placement. Before receiving a dog, 13% of farmers said they used lethal control; afterward, the figure fell to 8%. The authors described this as a modest reduction that could reflect changing attitudes toward wildlife. However, the survey cannot establish that the dogs alone caused the decline, and the results do not show that the program eliminated retaliatory killings.The dogs also faced considerable risks. Their average lifespan was 56 months, and 32% of recorded deaths occurred before age 2. Field accidents were the leading cause of death, with snake bites accounting for more than half of those accidents. Behavioral problems were reported in 28% of surveys, most commonly when dogs stayed at home instead of accompanying the herd.The program also carried potential costs for wildlife. Reports of dogs killing wild animals, mostly jackals, appeared in 41% of surveys. Most incidents involved individual animals, but a small number of surveys recorded 50 or more jackals killed. The authors said these ecological effects require further investigation, indicating that guarding dogs can reduce some risks to livestock while creating risks for wild animals.Some unwanted behaviors became less common over time. Dogs surveyed between 2010 and 2018 were 4.47 times less likely to chase game than those surveyed between 1994 and 2001. The researchers also emphasized the importance of proper care and early supervision in preventing or correcting unwanted behavior.The authors cautioned that the survey results may underestimate livestock losses. Respondents may also have given answers they believed interviewers wanted to hear, potentially affecting the findings. These limitations mean the reported reductions should be interpreted with care. Nevertheless, the researchers concluded that the program had been successful overall and recommended livestock guarding dogs for other areas experiencing similar livestock losses.

title: Sammy Obeid claims he was detained, refused entry in Japan; US comedian details experience
description: Sammy Obeid, the US comedian, claimed he was detained in Japan and refused entry, though he had shows scheduled there.
content: Sammy Obeid, the US comedian, claimed he was detained in Japan and refused entry, though he had shows scheduled there. Obeid shared his experience via a string of posts on X.“The Japanese government denied me entry and held me in solitary confinement for 24 hours over a standup comedy show with 40 attendees,” he wrote. The comedian said he was being sent back to the US and apologized to his fans. Japanese authorities have not issued a statement on the matter at the time of writing.Also Read | OutStation on India's Got Latent appearance, BTS influence: What they did for Korea, we want to do for IndiaObeid added that fans could either get a refund, transfer the ticket and catch his show elsewhere in the world, or stay tuned for a virtual show from the comedian. The 42-year-old shared the experience he faced.What Sammy Obeid claimed about his experience in JapanObeid claimed that he had arrived in Tokyo two days before his performance, with two other comedians who seemed to have entered without incident. However, when it came to him, the comedian claimed that his US passport was put in a ‘wrinkled plastic bag’ and he was taken to a ‘painfully lit holding room’.He was allegedly told that he was detained for ‘security reasons’ and that Japanese authorities needed more information for why he was there. Obeid went on to claim that authorities sought his ‘hour by hour’ plan while in Japan, and also asked for details of what he planned to do in the other countries he visited after Japan.The comedian appeared to blame Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for him being denied entry to Japan, but there is no substantiation to back this claim. He also claimed his luggage was searched for ‘weapons and drugs’, and that he was kept in solitary confinement for 22 hours, during which time, he had no access to food or shower.Why was Sammy Obeid detained?Obeid explained that he was detained due to a visa technicality. Authorities told him he had not arrived on the ‘right visa’ to be an entertainer. Obeid explained his difficulty in getting the specific eligibility criteria for the visa they spoke of.“Everyone I asked in the process was not able to get me the needed sponsorship. Also no one in Japan is paying me directly. Tickets are collected through a third party, US based app. So everyone I consulted with said I would be fine, as I had on previous trips. But I was not. And yea it's on me for not seeing this coming. But given everything I knew at the time, this was the best I could do to try to put on a show for the size crowd I have in Japan,” the comedian detailed.Obeid describes himself as ‘Lebanese-Palestinian-Syrian-Italian-American’ on his IMDb profile. Born in Oakland, California, he's best known for the 1,001 day streak of consecutive comedy performances.

title: Ondřej Surý: The man helping fix PHP’s security flaws speaks out amid website vulnerability fears
description: Volunteer maintainer Ondřej Surý helped speed distribution of fixes for two serious PHP vulnerabilities, which could let attackers run code on affected servers.
content: A volunteer software maintainer who helps distribute security fixes for PHP has emerged as a key figure in efforts to protect websites worldwide after two serious vulnerabilities triggered an urgent race to patch affected systems.Ondřej Surý, who lives in Czechia, helps maintain and automate software packages for PHP, a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites, according to The Atlantic. The vulnerabilities, disclosed earlier this week, could allow attackers to execute their own code on affected servers, potentially enabling them to steal data, disrupt websites or use compromised systems for criminal activity.The PHP Foundation, which maintains the programming language, had learned about the flaws before information about them was leaked online. The leak prompted developers to accelerate the release of a patch, bringing forward the timeline by a day. The incident highlighted concerns about how much of the internet depends on a relatively small number of people maintaining critical open-source software.Also Read: US issues travel alert ahead of Steelers vs Saints Paris NFL game as protests rock FrancePHP security flaws trigger race to release fixesThe vulnerabilities prompted a rapid response from the PHP project, software maintainers and website operators. After the patch was released, websites and organizations took systems offline to implement the fix, including government websites in Germany and Finland, as well as some hospital and school websites in Europe.Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities rose sharply around the public disclosure. He reported thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before the flaws were announced, followed by tens of thousands within 45 minutes, hundreds of thousands within two hours and millions subsequently.Surý’s contribution involves preparing PHP source code into packages that administrators can install on servers. These packages make it easier to deploy updates across large numbers of machines without having to compile the software manually.He told The Atlantic that he had been working in this area for more than 20 years and had time to prepare the packages before the fix was released. Although other sources could provide the PHP code, he said distributing ready-to-install packages made the process faster and easier for administrators.Also Read: US visa bulletin November 2026: Latest update brings selective progress for Indian green card applicantsVolunteer maintainers raise concerns about internet securitySurý does not work for the PHP Foundation. He volunteers on the project alongside his full-time role as director of domain-name-system engineering at the nonprofit Internet Systems Consortium. His work has received donations, but he said the contributions he normally receives are modest.Following the security incident, donations increased significantly. Surý said contributions received over 24 hours were equivalent to roughly a year’s worth of donations previously collected.He also said contingency plans were being discussed with Raphaël Hertzog of software company Freexian so that others could take over if he became unavailable.Surý warned that the risk had not disappeared because not every website had installed the updates. Unpatched systems could still face vandalism, disruption, botnet infections or cryptocurrency-mining abuse. He also rejected claims that older PHP versions were permanently impossible to patch, saying updates remained possible if operators took the necessary steps.Surý calls for better support for open-source softwareThe incident has renewed questions about whether companies and organizations invest enough in the infrastructure they rely on. Surý said artificial intelligence tools were accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities, but defenders could also use large language models to identify security weaknesses.He argued that businesses benefiting from open-source software should provide better financial support to the people maintaining it, warning that the current system could become unsustainable if volunteers lost motivation.For ordinary internet users, Surý recommended relying on cybersecurity experts during such incidents. He described the episode as another warning that critical digital infrastructure cannot be taken for granted.

title: In 1859, 13 rabbits were released in Australia for hunting; just 7 years later, more than 14,000 had been shot on the estate
description: In 1859, a settler freed 13 rabbits for hunting. Seven years later, 14,000 were shot, and rabbits spread across two-thirds of Australia in 50 years.
content: Sometimes small choices can end up reshaping a whole continent. The National Museum of Australia notes that on Christmas Day in 1859, Thomas Austin, a self-made man and wealthy settler, released 13 wild European rabbits on his estate in Victoria, Australia. The rabbits were let go for people to hunt for sport. By 1866, seven years after the release, hunters had shot 14,000 rabbits on the estate. The release marked the start of one of Australia's major pest problems.A gift from home that got out of handA relative in England had specifically collected the rabbits and sent them to Austin. Rabbits had been introduced to Australia before; five were on the First Fleet, but they were never released into the wild. Austin's rabbits were different. They went out and found lots of food, good ground cover, and no predators. Those conditions helped the rabbits spread quickly. By 1880, they were over the Murray River into New South Wales. By 1886, they were in Queensland. By 1894, they were over the Nullarbor Plain and had settled Western Australia. It took rabbits 700 years to colonize Britain, but they spread through two-thirds of Australia in just 50 years, which the museum describes as the fastest spread of a colonizing mammal anywhere in the world.Fences, viruses and a long fightSettlers and governments tried many ways to fight back, including trapping, fumigation, and bounty systems, but fences were the most visible method. The most iconic one was Western Australia's rabbit-proof fence, built between 1901 and 1907. It extended 3,256 kilometers (about 2,023 miles) north to south across the state. The fence was unsuccessful partly because it was completed after rabbits had already crossed into the state, and the fence kept deteriorating, so there was almost always somewhere to cross. Rabbits, too, were a free source of meat in lean years, and during the 1930s Depression, many people shot them for food or trapped them. Later scientists started to look at disease. In 1950, trials with myxomatosis, a virus that affects rabbits, were renewed, and the disease spread at incredible speed after rain brought more mosquitoes. But the rabbits began to develop resistance, just as they later did to the virus known as calicivirus. Their numbers are now on the rise again.What rabbits do to the landThe damage goes beyond farms. The museum says rabbits will eat just about anything that grows. Over time, very large numbers can overgraze and damage native plants and the native animals that depend on them. Heavy grazing can also lead to soil erosion.In a 2012 paper in Wildlife Research, Brian Cooke of the University of Canberra examined the rabbit’s place in Australian ecosystems. His review notes that wild rabbits have degraded many natural Australian ecosystems and any beneficial role they play is small by comparison. Cooke also concluded that rabbits could be controlled adequately to begin restoration of the ecosystem, but that a high level of control was necessary.Why this story still mattersBy the late 1940s, rabbit numbers had climbed to 600 million. The author Brian Coman, quoted by the museum, calls the rabbit the country's most serious vertebrate pest. Austin's release was meant to add a little sport to his estate. Instead, it became a lesson in how quickly an introduced animal can take over when food, cover, and few predators are in alignment. It is also a warning against moving animals to places where the local ecosystem has no natural defenses against them.

title: Researchers enrolled 182 pet dog teams to see if they could sniff out hidden spotted lanternfly eggs, a costly invasive pest threatening crops
description: Volunteer pet dogs and their owners trained to sniff out spotted lanternfly eggs. A PeerJ study found many passed, though the dropout rate was high.
content: Spotted lanternfly egg masses typically contain 30 to 50 eggs and can be deposited on trees, rocks, outdoor equipment, and other surfaces, making them difficult to spot during inspections. Dogs may be able to detect these hidden egg masses by scent, even when they are not visible to inspectors. In a 2025 study published in PeerJ, Sally Dickinson and colleagues investigated whether companion dogs with scent-detection training could help identify the eggs and support efforts to limit the insect's spread.Native to parts of Asia, including China and Vietnam, the spotted lanternfly was first detected in Pennsylvania in 2014, likely after arriving on a shipment of landscaping stone. The invasive planthopper faces fewer natural enemies in parts of the United States where it has established populations and feeds on grapevines, hops, and ornamental plants, posing a threat to agriculture and other vegetation. Its egg masses can adhere to wood, stone, and other materials that people transport, allowing the insect to spread to new areas. Although specially trained detection dogs are already used to locate spotted lanternfly eggs, their limited numbers can restrict their availability. The researchers explored whether companion dogs could help expand detection efforts.Serious training for companion dogsResearchers at Texas Tech University and Virginia Tech recruited participants through Facebook, receiving 1,033 responses. Of those respondents, 427 said their dogs already had scent-detection training, and 182 dog-handler teams from across the United States enrolled in the study. The dogs included Labradors, border collies, poodles, and other breeds.Training used frozen egg masses rather than live specimens. Researchers collected spotted lanternfly eggs at the Virginia Tech Agricultural Research and Extension Center in Winchester, Virginia, and stored them at minus 80 degrees Celsius for at least 30 days to render them nonviable. They placed 0.5 grams of the treated eggs in stainless steel mesh packets, sealed the packets in Mylar bags, and shipped them to trainers. Owners then spent three to six months teaching their dogs to recognize the scent, without following a single prescribed training method.The researchers assessed the teams through two tests. In the box test, each dog searched a semicircle of six boxes. One could contain the target eggs, while the others held distractors such as tree bark or a medical glove. The dog had 90 seconds to locate the target or indicate that no eggs were present. Teams needed at least eight successful trials out of 10 to pass. During the field test, dogs searched an area measuring at least 25 by 25 meters for three to five samples within five minutes. Promising results, actual limitationsThe results showed that some companion dogs could detect the egg masses under controlled and field conditions. In the box test, 77 of 104 team attempts met the passing criteria. Dogs detected the eggs in 82% of trials in which they were present, and 87% of their alerts were correct. The field test was more challenging, with a sensitivity of 58%. This means the dogs detected the eggs in slightly more than half of the instances in which they were present. However, 56 of the 66 field-test attempts passed, and 91% of the dogs' alerts were correct. Wind and temperature were not significantly associated with test success.A smaller group of teams then attempted to detect live egg masses. After a two-minute warm-up with the target odor, 22 of the 24 teams available for this test passed.
