The result suggests that dogs trained with frozen samples can also recognize live eggs, potentially allowing handlers to train without transporting viable specimens that could contribute to the pest's spread.Participation declined substantially during the study. Although 182 teams enrolled, only 104 attempts were recorded for the box test, and 24 teams were available for the live-egg trial. Many participants withdrew before completing their first test, often citing scheduling difficulties and time constraints. The dogs and handlers also had trouble identifying when no eggs were present. They sometimes took longer to respond or incorrectly alerted to a distractor. In addition, the researchers did not compare field-test outcomes between teams that passed the box test and those that failed, leaving it unclear whether performance in the controlled setting predicted success outdoors.The findings suggest that companion dogs could supplement existing spotted lanternfly detection efforts, although further evaluation is needed before their wider use can be established. The researchers proposed that trained volunteers could eventually help inspect shipments or search orchards, with any canine alert prompting a closer examination by human inspectors. Funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the project provides an initial assessment of whether pet dogs can contribute to the detection of an invasive pest.

title: After cats wiped out flightless rails on Aldabra’s Picard Island, 18 birds were returned in 1999; by 2012, nearly 3,000 lived there
description: In 1999, 18 Aldabra rails, the last flightless bird in the Indian Ocean, returned to Picard Island after cats were gone. By 2012, nearly 3,000 lived there.
content: A bird that cannot fly has one big problem when a predator shows up: nowhere to go. On Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles, that predator was cats, and they were the main reason a flightless bird vanished from two of the atoll’s islands. In a 2013 study published in the journal Conservation Evidence Šúr, van de Crommenacker and Bunbury examined the return of that bird, the Aldabra rail, to Picard Island. It began with 18 birds and a reintroduction plan that exceeded scientists’ expectations.Why the rail lost its homeŠúr and colleagues describe the Aldabra rail as the last surviving flightless bird in the Indian Ocean. Cats were a serious threat because a flightless bird has no quick way out. The study suggests that the rail disappeared from Grande Terre before the late 1800s and from Picard shortly after 1910. In both cases, the main culprit was feral cats brought in by early settlers. By 1998, the rail existed on only three of the atoll's islands, and Picard was not among them. That left the entire wild population confined to three islands of a single atoll. A careful plan to bring it backOnce the cats were off Picard, the island could be a home again. Wanless and colleagues documented the effort in a 2002 Biological Conservation paper, which notes that 18 rails were reintroduced there in 1999. The team used a soft release, which means the birds were given time and support to adjust to their new surroundings before being left on their own. They came from nearby Malabar Island, were moved while pairs were forming, and reached Picard within three days. The birds were then placed in enclosures of about 320 square feet near suitable habitat, with shelter, fresh water, and food, for six to 14 days. Even after release, the team continued to provide food to birds that stayed near their cages.Early results were promising Monitoring showed that all 18 released birds survived from November 1999 until at least April 2000. Seventeen birds were re-sighted between December 2000 and April 2001, and the remaining bird was recorded in an inaccessible part of the island. The rails were breeding as well. All chick deaths known in the first season happened within three weeks of hatching. The team figured that 15 to 16 chicks fledged, meaning they got old enough to leave the nest, in the first season, and at least 20 more did so in the second. By 2001, the number of birds on Picard had risen to at least 51, up from the original 18.From 18 birds to nearly 3,000Scientists had predicted that Picard could hold about 1,000 pairs of rails by 2010, which they saw as the island’s limit. A follow-up survey 12 years after the release, one year after the predicted population peak, confirmed that Picard had reached that limit and likely surpassed it. It found about 1,106 territorial pairs, roughly 10% more than predicted, plus an estimated 553 non-breeding adults, or about 2,765 birds in all. By 2012, the Seychelles Islands Foundation, which manages Aldabra, estimated the population at close to 3,000 birds. That’s a big jump from 18, but not every reintroduction will be like this. This was one species on one island, and the cats had to go first. The study also offers a reliable way to count rails and recommends continued monitoring and conservation management. For a bird that can’t fly away from trouble, Picard became a true second chance.

title: In 2025, California DNA analysis suggested Oregon may be linked to the state’s renewed nutria invasion after the rodents reappeared in 2017
description: A genomic study of 267 California nutria points to central Oregon and a recent introduction rather than a long-hidden group.
content: In 2017, a pregnant female nutria was captured in a private wetland near Gustine in Merced County, California. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife says nutria had been declared eradicated from the state by 1978, with no reported detections between then and their rediscovery. During the summer of 2017, officials captured 19 additional nutria in the Grasslands Ecological Area.A 2025 study published in Evolutionary Applications found that California’s current nutria population was genetically most similar to invasive nutria in central Oregon. The findings suggest a recent introduction followed by rapid spread, although the genetic evidence cannot establish the precise route by which the animals reached California.The invasion threatens wetlands and agricultural land in the Central Valley, where nutria can damage vegetation, undermine streambanks and levees, and contribute to soil erosion. To investigate the animals’ origins, researchers analyzed 6,809 genetic markers from 267 California nutria sampled between 2020 and 2022. They compared the results with genetic data from populations in Oregon, Washington, Louisiana, Texas, Maryland, and Virginia. The study also examined historical museum specimens to assess whether the current population might descend from earlier nutria populations in California.DNA resultsThe California nutria formed a distinct genetic cluster, but their closest relatives came from central Oregon, while nutria from northern Oregon were genetically linked to Washington. Scientists also examined maternally inherited DNA and found that all California nutria shared the same marker, which also appeared in nutria from Oregon and Washington.Historical specimens provided a way to compare the current population with nutria from earlier decades. Researchers sequenced pelts, skulls, and bones from California fur farm animals, with most specimens dating from 1930 to 1960. The older specimens had four variants of the maternal DNA marker, indicating greater diversity than the single variant found in the current population. One of the historical variants matched the marker found in modern California nutria.However, this genetic overlap does not establish that the present population descended from animals that survived undetected in the state. Because the historical and current populations shared a maternal marker, the evidence alone cannot determine whether the earlier population persisted or whether nutria were introduced again. The authors considered a recent introduction followed by rapid spread more likely, given California’s favorable climate and the animals’ reproductive potential. What do officials think about it?In an April 7, 2026, news release, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said the genetic findings suggest that the current invasion resulted from an intentional reintroduction, with the animals likely transported from central Oregon. Transporting nutria is prohibited under California Fish and Game Code Section 2118 and Title 14, Section 671, of the California Code of Regulations. The genetic analysis supports the hypothesis of a recent introduction, but it does not identify who transported the animals or establish the circumstances behind their release.Since 2017, California’s Nutria Eradication Program has removed 7,841 nutria, the department reported. Officials estimated that eradication efforts cost the state about $5 million annually. Teams search hundreds of thousands of acres of wetland and riparian habitat from San Pablo Bay to Kings County, using direct observation, motion-detection cameras, and fecal-detection dogs to locate animals for trapping.The study also offers guidance for eradication efforts. Because researchers found little genetic differentiation across the invaded range, they argued that managers could treat the Central Valley as a single eradication unit. River distance appeared to matter more than straight-line distance in explaining gene flow, suggesting that waterways help nutria move through the landscape. Access to affected areas also poses a challenge because much of the invaded range is privately owned, and some wetlands cannot be trapped during hunting and nesting seasons.To trace the population’s origins, researcher Kristen Ahrens contacted museums and universities across California to obtain historical specimens. One unusual contribution came from the Butte County Weights and Measures Department, which provided a taxidermied nutria. Ahrens also reported that the research team had developed a global genetic reference database to help other scientists compare nutria populations and investigate invasion routes. The project received funding from the California Department of Water Resources in cooperation with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

title: Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano charged after Iwo Jima statue at Quantico Marine base vandalized with sledgehammer
description: Authorities alleged that the 27-year-old Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano beheaded one of the six Marines depicted in the World War II memorial.
content: Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano has been charged after authorities alleged he used a sledgehammer to behead one of the Marines depicted in a replica of the iconic Iwo Jima memorial at the US Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. The damage caused by the vandalism is estimated to be of hundreds of thousands of dollars.According to law enforcement, Maldonado Soriano, 27, was arrested around 10:15 pm on Wednesday. Officers allegedly found him striking the monument with a sledgehammer at the Marine Corps installation, located about 36 miles south of Washington, DC.Authorities said one of the six servicemen represented in the memorial was decapitated during the attack. Additional sections of the limestone monument were also damaged.Maldonado Soriano has been charged with felony destruction of property, trespassing with intent to damage property and felony injury to a monument, according to police. He is being held without bond.Also read: Matthew Modabber: Polymarket top executive's firing reportedly angered CEO and school friend Shayne CoplanInvestigation continues as officials assess damageAuthorities said preliminary estimates place the damage to the Quantico monument in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.Officials have not publicly disclosed a possible motive for the alleged vandalism.Soriano entered the country illegally in December 1999, according to federal sources. He was given DACA in 2014 by the Obama administration and had it extended for many years, most recently by the Biden administration in 2024. However, he lost his DACA status in August of this year when the Trump administration failed to renew it.In a statement to The New York Post, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers stated, “This criminal illegal alien’s dream is over: Maldonado Soriano disrespected our brave service members and defaced a beautiful monument that honored their sacrifice.”Rogers continued, "President Trump has secured our border and is deporting illegal criminals who hate our country and our values. The socialist Democrats want to go back to open borders and flood our communities with dangerous criminal illegal aliens.Also read: Major US medical lab operator, Quest Diagnostics, reports cyber breach exposed patient recordsReplica honors Marines who died in serviceThe damaged monument is a replica of the famed Marine Corps War Memorial, which commemorates the US flag raising atop Mount Suribachi during the Battle of Iwo Jima in February 1945, one of the defining moments of World War II.The original memorial in Arlington, Virginia, was sculpted by Felix de Weldon and dedicated in 1954. It honors all Marines who have died in service to the United States since 1775, according to the US Marine Corps.The Marine Corps War Memorial remains one of the nation’s best-known military monuments. It is also home to several historic memorials dedicated to Marine Corps history and service.

title: In 1998, Przewalski's horses were brought to Chernobyl; by 2018, researchers counted 137 in Ukraine's exclusion zone despite early deaths and poaching
description: In 1998, rare Przewalski’s horses were brought to Chernobyl. Despite early deaths and poaching, 2018 camera traps counted 137 in Ukraine’s exclusion zone.
content: Chernobyl is known as a place people had to flee. Yet in 1998, a conservation program brought a rare wild horse there on purpose. A 2019 study by Sergii Gashchak and Sergii Paskevych, published in Theriologia Ukrainica, used camera traps in 2018 and counted 137 Przewalski's horses in the Ukrainian part of the exclusion zone. That number is more impressive when you look at how the story started. Poaching and early losses took their toll, but the herd survived.A wild horse gets a new homePrzewalski's horse is a rare wild horse found in open steppe landscapes. In 1998, the Askania Nova Biosphere Reserve initiated a program to establish a free-ranging herd in the Chernobyl exclusion zone. The aim was to help restore the area’s biodiversity. According to a 2008 paper by Zharkikh and Yasynetska, 31 horses were transferred there in 1998 and 1999. Ten males and 18 females were from Askania Nova, and three males were from a local zoo. Horses were kept in enclosures for a few weeks to eight months before release.A tough first chapterThe project got off to a difficult start. Eight horses died while being transported, or soon after, the same paper noted. The surviving original group bred well, and between 1999 and 2003 the population grew, peaking at 65 horses in 2003 and 2004. In 2004, another 13 horses from city zoos were released without a settling-in period. They failed to adapt, and soon died out, without offspring. By October 2007, the number had decreased to between 30 and 40 horses. The authors report that over 70 percent of all deaths with a known cause were due to illegal hunting. They also found that wolves and disease had little effect on the herd. The comeback and the 2018 countThe herd did not vanish. In 2018, Gashchak and Paskevych’s camera traps recorded 137 horses in the Ukrainian zone. Among them were 47 stallions, 66 mares and young females, and 24 foals. The team surveyed up to 720 square kilometers of the 2,600-square-kilometer zone, so the true total was probably higher. They also spotted at least four more horses at a remote location in the Belarusian part of the zone. The authors say the herd’s current demographic indicators show no negative trends. Some horses crossed the Prypiat River between 2007 and 2010 and established a new breeding group. But growth did slow. The rate of increase between 2009 and 2018 was about one-third lower than between 1998 and 2008. The authors say this was likely due to the changing age composition of the herd, as the first group consisted only of mature, more productive mares, while younger, less productive mares became more common over time.Why cameras helpThe wild horses are not easy to count. Gashchak and Paskevych say forests are taking over old meadows and sightings in the woods are rare. Cameras help. A 2020 study by Schlichting, Dombrovski, and Beasley in Mammal Research placed cameras at the entrances of abandoned buildings. In the winter of 2016 to 2017, horses were seen 35 times at nine of the ten monitored buildings. In the summer of 2018, they were detected 149 times at all eight buildings monitored that season. The horses were more likely to come at night in winter and at dawn and dusk in summer. The authors say this method could help monitor the herd, whose size and genetic diversity were unknown at the time.What it meansThis is not a simple happy ending. At least two males in the 2019 study showed signs of interbreeding with domestic horses. Zharkikh and Yasynetska also warned that killing off some of the early horses’ offspring could reduce genetic diversity. But the numbers are encouraging. A herd that fell to 30 to 40 horses in 2007 was counted at 137 in 2018. It shows that a small herd can bounce back, though it still needs careful watching.

title: In 1933, a hurricane devastated Virginia’s Hog Island; 45 years later, conservationists found the sheep left there thriving and took them to safety
description: After a 1933 hurricane, people left Virginia’s Hog Island, but its sheep survived in the wild. In 1978, conservationists found them thriving and moved them.
content: Have you ever had a plan fall apart and then watched things turn out better than expected? A flock of sheep on Virginia’s Hog Island lived something like that, and it surprised the people who found them. The story is told by the Livestock Conservancy, a non-profit organization dedicated to protecting rare farm breeds, on its Hog Island sheep page. In 1933, a hurricane destroyed the island, and its inhabitants gradually left, but many sheep were left behind and survived in the wild. In 1978, conservationists discovered that the flock was thriving and animals were moved to safety.An island flock with deep rootsHog Island is a barrier island located off the coast of Virginia. For hundreds of years, small groups of people and livestock have lived there. The Livestock Conservancy says that in the 1700s a flock was formed from local sheep of British origin. Life on the island had made them hardy, good at finding food, and able to reproduce successfully. Some outside breeding was introduced over time, but isolation and natural selection still shaped the flock into a distinct breed. At their peak in the early 1900s, there were hundreds of sheep. They ranged at will, eating marsh grass and drinking fresh water from shallow pools dug in the sandy soil.A hurricane devastated the islandAll of Hog Island was flooded in a 1933 hurricane, according to the USGS report, Coasts in Crisis. It destroyed much of the town of Broadwater and killed the pine forest that shielded the island. Then, in the 1930s, a string of hurricanes and nor’easters discouraged people from staying. By 1945, all residents had relocated to Virginia’s Eastern Shore, taking most of their livestock with them. But many sheep were left behind. They continued to live as they had lived for centuries, eating marsh grass and finding fresh water for themselves. After the move, spring shearing and notching were usually the only time owners and sheep met. A surprise discovery in 1978The Nature Conservancy bought the island in 1974. Four years later, Virginia Coast Reserve agents found a thriving flock there, much to their surprise. The flock's survival is a testament to the animals' resilience. In late August 1978, the Nature Conservancy took the sheep off the island, with the idea of returning them to full domestication. The animals were taken from the island and placed in managed care. Ten rams and 20 ewes were sent to Virginia Tech to study the breed's parasite resistance.From island survivors to living historyIn a yearlong study, it turned out that it was not resistance that had kept the sheep almost parasite-free on the island, but isolation. After their stay at the university, the remnant flock moved to George Washington’s Birthplace National Monument. Today, some flocks are still in the hands of private breeders, and many Hog Island sheep live at living history museums in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, the Livestock Conservancy reports. That makes sense because the sheep resemble British sheep that lived in the New World during and after the colonial period. Most have white wool and about 20 percent are black. Adult weight ranges from about 90 pounds to 150 pounds.Why the story continues to matterHog Island sheep show how animals can adjust to their environment. They are self-sufficient, good foragers that prefer browsing over grazing, according to the Livestock Conservancy. The breed's critical status means its future still depends on breeders and conservationists. Every museum flock and private breeder contributes to moving the breed forward. It began with a hurricane and a barrier island and continues today in living history museums and on breeders' farms.

title: In 1874, rabbits reached the remote Kerguelen Islands; later research found two sensitive native plants had disappeared from grazed areas
description: Rabbits brought to the Kerguelen Islands in 1874 wiped out sensitive native plants in grazed areas, and two studies show recovery is slow even after removal.
content: Rabbits are usually seen as harmless, like a fluffy pet or a cartoon character, but on a faraway island chain, they changed the landscape in ways that scientists are still studying. A 2004 study in Biological Conservation by Jean-Louis Chapuis, Yves Frenot, and Marc Lebouvier found that the introduction of rabbits in 1874 had a major impact on the plant life of the Kerguelen archipelago. The most sensitive native plants, the Kerguelen cabbage and the cushion plant, disappeared from grazed areas.A remote island chain and a risky ideaThe Kerguelen Islands lie in the southern Indian Ocean. The French first recorded the islands in 1772, and today a small group of scientists and engineers live there. There are no airports, so everything and everyone comes by boat. In the past, the islands were a stop for whale and seal-hunting ships. People tried to make the place friendlier by bringing animals and plants from home at different times.In 1874, someone brought European rabbits to the islands, probably as a food source. Nothing there hunted them. As a result, the rabbits bred quickly and ate large amounts of vegetation. Their burrows also made the soil more susceptible to erosion, allowing non-native plants to move in.What the 2004 study foundOf the 29 plant species native to Kerguelen, few remained in rabbit-grazed areas. The cushion plant and the Kerguelen cabbage, the most sensitive species, became scarce or disappeared. Acaena magellanica took over most coastal areas and formed almost single-species communities. The team also examined how the vegetation recovered. The rabbit eradication program began on Île Verte in 1992 and on Île Guillou in 1994. Afterward, the number of plant species rose on both islands. Some native plants, mainly Acaena magellanica, lost cover, while non-native plants, especially dandelions, spread. Other native plants showed signs of increasing, but later work suggests that full recovery is slow.The damage hiding in the soilA later study published in 2015 in Biology Letters, led by Johan Pansu, looked beneath the surface. Fungi are a natural part of a healthy soil community, so the team took soil samples from three islands and searched for fungal DNA. On Grande Terre, there are rabbits everywhere. On Grande Terre, rabbits are widespread. Rabbits were removed from Île Guillou in 1994. Île Australia never had any.The fungi on Île Australia and at a rabbit site on Grande Terre were very different. That mirrored differences in their plants. There were lots of native plants on Île Australia. The Grande Terre site was dominated by Acaena magellanica and non-native dandelions. Here's the surprise: even after 20 years without rabbits, plant and fungal communities at Île Guillou remained similar to those at the rabbit site. The researchers suggest this reflects slow recovery of the native vegetation after the rabbits were removed.What the findings suggestThe rabbits weren't some evil villains set out to destroy the world. Humans introduced them, and they ended up becoming an invasive threat. The islands paid a price that is still visible decades later. The two studies together tie one introduced animal to changes in plants, soil erosion, and soil fungi. They also suggest that recovery can take a long time even when the animal is gone.These results are from specific sites on the Kerguelen Islands and thus do not show that all islands will respond in the same manner. Nature does not always heal fast, so it is best to be cautious about moving species from one place to another.

title: In 1807, a captain left pigs on New Zealand’s Auckland Islands for future sailors; in 1999, 17 were rescued, while feral pigs remained on the island
description: In 1807, a captain left pigs for castaways on a remote island. In 1999, 17 were rescued; wild pigs remain a medical resource and an environmental problem.
content: A little act of kindness can cast a very long shadow. In 1807, a sea captain left pigs on a distant island for the benefit of future sailors. More than two hundred years later, people are still arguing about the pigs of the Auckland Islands. In a 2022 paper in the New Zealand Journal of Ecology, Michael Trotter and Michael Willis reviewed how livestock arrived at these subantarctic islands south of mainland New Zealand and the fate of the pigs.A captain’s gift for castawaysCaptain Abraham Bristow found the islands in 1806 but did not land. He returned a year later and stayed on the islands for two months. In 1810 he wrote a letter saying he had left a breed of hogs on Enderby Island for the benefit of future navigators. Livestock arrived on the islands to feed castaways or to be farmed, the study explains. Ships did wreck there, including the Grafton in 1864, and the General Grant in 1866. Survivors of the General Grant later caught pigs on Auckland Island.The pigs weren’t staying put. A United States expedition in March 1840 spent some days in the north of Auckland Island and saw no pigs. In November and December of that year, Captain James Clark Ross found many running wild there and left more. Ross believed the pigs were from Bristow’s hogs, but the authors noted that this was not certain, since the animals may have swum over from Enderby Island. When the survivors of the General Grant were rescued, they turned their remaining pigs loose on Enderby Island for the benefit of others. Those pigs were dead or killed off by 1887, but the wild pigs on the larger Auckland Island itself survived. The 1999 rescue and its medical valueConservation officials called the pigs on Auckland Island a threat to the environment and planned to remove them. A rare-breeds group had already stepped in to save a living sample. The team left Bluff Harbour, on the southern coast of New Zealand’s South Island, for the Auckland Islands on January 12, 1999. Trained dogs tracked the pigs through thick forest, and handlers taped the pigs’ legs and jaws before carrying them to the shore. In the end, 17 pigs were caught on Auckland Island and taken to New Zealand. The authors mentioned their calm temperaments, and their tails generally ended in a tassel, while several had almost woolly ears. DNA studies showed they were a separate breed and closest in type to European pigs.The rescue also had medical benefits. Samples from the pigs were sent to labs around the world and returned free of a virus that worried researchers studying pig-to-human transplants. The pigs were first studied as a possible source of cells to treat diabetes. The breed has been a valuable source of medical products, the study reports. But it is a small group. Neither the pigs in the biosecure facility nor those elsewhere in the country are likely to number more than 30 mature animals. A separate genetic study found low variability compared with other pigs.Pigs that stayed behindWild pigs also stayed on Auckland Island. Stephen Horn and colleagues reported in a 2022 feasibility study that it was the only island in New Zealand’s subantarctic region that still had introduced mammalian pests: pigs, mice and cats. They found that removing all three was worthwhile and feasible, but that it depended on further development of new technology. Decision makers delayed the work in 2020 because of the economic effects of COVID-19. The issue split people. Trotter and Willis wrote that the pigs do cause some environmental damage, but argued their human value could be of huge global benefit and their genetic material should be preserved. That left the island pigs both a medical resource and an environmental problem, depending on whom you asked.

title: From 1982 to 1987, Israel reintroduced 28 Asiatic wild asses to the Negev; after 10 more were released in 1992 and 1993, the herd reached about 250
description: Israel reintroduced Asiatic wild asses to the Negev in 1982, and the herd grew to about 250, but a 2018 study warns that uneven mating limits genetic diversity.
content: Few animals vanish from a desert and then find their way back. The Asiatic wild ass did, with human help. According to a 2018 study in Conservation Biology, 28 wild asses were released into Israel’s Negev from a captive herd between 1982 and 1987. Another ten were released in 1992 and 1993. Since then, the herd has grown, which sounds like a clear win. But a growing herd is not always a healthy one.How the wild ass disappeared and came backThe Asiatic wild ass lived on the desert steppes of Mongolia, Russia, and the Arabian Peninsula. Today it survives in small isolated groups. In the Negev, it was gone by the 1920s, according to a 2013 article from Washington University in St. Louis. Because the animal could not be tamed, the local Bedouin hunted it for its meat. Alan Templeton, an evolutionary biologist, says water and World War I finished it off. In summer, nursing mothers must drink daily, but the displaced people settled near the few permanent sources of water and kept the asses at a distance. Without water, the mothers couldn’t raise their foals.The comeback began with a small herd that survived in the Shah of Iran’s zoo. In 1968, animals from that herd were brought to the Hai-Bar Yotvata Reserve in Israel and bred there. The captive group did well. The same article says blood tests showed very high genetic diversity. Shirli Bar David of Ben-Gurion University recognized the parallel to Templeton’s work with collared lizards in Missouri. Both species were reintroduced beginning in the early 1980s from small founding populations: 29 lizards and, eventually, 38 wild asses. Studying a herd that avoids peopleBy 2005, little was known about how the released animals were faring. They were hard to find, and they stayed away from people. Bar David, Amos Bouskila, and Templeton went to see for themselves. They used methods that disturbed the animals as little as possible. They counted the animals at watering holes during the summer. Many of the animals can be identified by coat markings and battle scars. The count revealed that the herd had increased from 38 to about 250. They also took DNA swabs from dung and put a GPS collar on a dominant male named Tail-less. He spent almost all of his time in a region about two kilometers wide. Every other week, he raced off on an exploratory trip and then returned.DNA from about 400 dung samples showed that the eastern group was already genetically distinct from the rest. Templeton says the asses avoid steep slopes. So they make long detours around the huge erosion craters of the Negev. Those craters seem to have kept the groups apart.Why a larger herd isn’t always a healthier herdNumbers are as important as genes. A 2015 study in Molecular Ecology examined the mating habits of asses. Genetic data were collected non-invasively, and computer modeling was used. It found that fewer than 25% of males participate in mating each generation. The 2018 Conservation Biology study then measured the herd’s effective population size. This number tells us how fast a group loses genetic diversity by chance. The result was 24.3, far below the herd’s total population. Among the factors the team examined, uneven mating had the strongest effect on how fast the herd loses genetic diversity. The authors call the low number a concern, even though the herd keeps growing.Males set up territories around water sources and typically maintain them through summer, the breeding season. So the authors propose adding more artificial water sources that could allow more males to gain territory and mate. That is a suggestion, not a proven solution. Templeton also notes that the zoo animals were hybrids of two of the five recognized subspecies. There are no more subspecies native to the Negev, so the team accepted that mix. He says the goal is a population that can keep evolving, not just one that survives.

title: Elon Musk invests $1 billion in CNN-owner Skydance: Report
description: The investment comes after Skydance looks to strengthen its finances after its Paramount merger.
content: Elon Musk has invested roughly $1 billion in Skydance, Semafor reported on Thursday. Musk's alleged investment provided a major financial boost to the Hollywood studio as it seeks to cut costs, strengthen its balance sheet and accelerate its technology strategy following its merger with Paramount, according to the report by Semafor.The investment was made alongside additional equity contributions from existing Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs, the publication reported. The funding comes after reports last month that Skydance was exploring an equity investment from Musk.Also read: Elon Musk allegedly reduced Ashley St Clair's child support from $100,000 to $20,000 after she revealed their sonMusk, Ellison ties fuel partnership speculationMusk has publicly praised Skydance chief executive David Ellison and Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison. This led to speculation that the investment could pave the way for broader collaboration between Skydance and Musk’s companies.According to Semafor, industry observers have speculated that Starlink, Musk’s satellite internet business, could eventually partner with Skydance as traditional television distribution shifts toward streaming.Cable billionaire John Malone also suggested such a partnership may emerge.“He’s gonna have to re-engineer all of those channels, and figure out how they morph into streams themselves rather than just traditional linear,” Malone said during an appearance at the Paley Center, according to Semafor.Malone also pointed to the long-standing relationship between Musk and the Ellison family. “Who helped Elon finance Twitter when he bought it? Larry Ellison,” Malone pointed out. He added that Larry Ellison previously used Tesla stock to help finance Skydance.Earlier this month, David Ellison outlined Skydance’s technology ambitions during a CNBC interview. “We are building a true product and tech team,” Ellison said. “We are a big believer that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists, not the other way around.”Also read: Elon Musk says ‘people will find ways to be happy’ if AI makes money and work obsolete in futureInvestment follows major Hollywood consolidationInvestors overwhelmingly approved Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros last month, which is a deal valued at about $111 billion that is expected to reshape Hollywood, according to The Telegraph.Unions have accused Ellison and his son David of editorial meddling following a series of cuts and adjustments to programming, notably on the company's signature news program 60 Minutes.Earlier this year, Christiane Amanpour, CNN's longtime chief international anchor, denounced the "destruction, potentially" of 60 Minutes and the "ideological realignment of CBS." CNN's previous director general, Mark Thompson, has also insisted that Skydance “both understand and will completely embrace the philosophy and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for.”

title: Jonathan Alan Lefman: Massachusetts family man convicted of abusive sexual contact with minor on flight
description: A federal jury convicted Jonathan Alan Lefman, 48, of repeatedly sexually touching a 17-year-old passenger without consent during a 2024 JetBlue flight.
content: A Massachusetts man has been convicted of repeatedly sexually touching a 17-year-old female passenger aboard a JetBlue flight from Puerto Rico to Boston in August 2024, with a federal jury finding him guilty after a three-day trial.Jonathan Alan Lefman, 48, of Newton, Massachusetts, was convicted on October 16 of one count of abusive sexual contact within the special aircraft jurisdiction of the United States, the US Department of Justice said on October 22. He was travelling with his wife and four children when the incident occurred, according to prosecutors.US District Court Judge Julia E. Kobick has scheduled Lefman's sentencing for January 12, 2027. The offence carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison, up to five years to life of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000.How the incident unfolded aboard the JetBlue flightAccording to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts, the incident took place on August 30, 2024, during a JetBlue flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Boston.Also Read: US issues travel alert ahead of Steelers vs Saints Paris NFL game as protests rock FranceProsecutors said Lefman repeatedly reached between the back and bottom of the seat directly in front of him, where the teenager was sitting, and touched her buttocks without her consent. The conduct allegedly continued during the flight and while passengers were waiting to leave the aircraft after it landed in Boston.On one occasion, the teenager saw Lefman's reflection leaning between the seats on the seatback monitor in front of her, according to the Justice Department.During another incident, she used her mobile phone camera to record a video showing Lefman's fingers protruding between the back and bottom of her seat. After leaving the aircraft, she also recorded a video of him on the jet bridge.The teenager's adult female family member, who had been travelling in a different row, subsequently reported the conduct to a JetBlue supervisor and confronted Lefman, showing the video as evidence, prosecutors said.US officials praise victim's courageUS Attorney Leah B. Foley said the verdict held Lefman accountable for repeatedly sexually abusing a minor who was trying to travel safely aboard a commercial flight.Also Read: US visa bulletin November 2026: Latest update brings selective progress for Indian green card applicants“No one should have to fear being sexually assaulted, whether in the air or on the ground,” Foley said in a statement released by the Justice Department.Ted E. Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI's Boston Division, also praised the teenager's courage in reporting the incident and helping bring the case to trial.The investigation involved the FBI and Massachusetts State Police, with assistance from the Boston Police Department. Assistant US Attorneys Elianna J. Nuzum and Julissa Walsh prosecuted the case.Sentencing scheduled for January 2027Lefman was arrested and charged in February 2025 before a federal grand jury indicted him in March that year. His conviction followed the jury trial concluded on October 16, 2026.The sentencing hearing is scheduled for January 12, 2027. The judge will determine the sentence based on federal sentencing guidelines and the applicable statutes.The conviction underscores the federal government's authority to prosecute qualifying sexual offences committed aboard commercial aircraft operating within US jurisdiction.

title: ‘He put it back’: Trump sidesteps question on calling Musk as Zelenskyy says Ukraine’s Starlink speed not fully restored
description: A slowdown in SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network last week disrupted Ukraine’s drone operations against the Russian army.
content: United States President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Ukraine’s Starlink internet access was restored by Elon Musk after the satellite service disruptions last week affected the country’s drone operations against the Russian army.Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump declined to comment whether he had personally contacted Musk over the issue and said, “It was a very interesting situation. I don’t want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called doesn’t make any difference. I guess the bottom line, he put it back.” However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday said that Starlink speed had not been fully restored for Ukraine, reported Reuters.“The speed has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet,” Zelenskyy said speaking at a press conference. "We are working on it,” he added. Ukraine relies on Starlink to maintain satellite connectivity for dronesA slowdown in SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network that disrupted Ukraine’s drone operations was triggered by an order from company's CEO Elon Musk, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing unnamed US officials and other sources. The move reportedly restricted Ukraine’s access to the satellite service, affecting the country’s ability to conduct both defensive and offensive drone missions against Russian forces.Ukraine relies on Starlink, operated by Musk’s space technology company SpaceX, to maintain satellite connectivity for drones used to intercept Russian attack drones as well as those deployed in strikes against Moscow.ALSO READ: Starlink and the digital sovereignty questionThe disruption affected drone operations and resulted in the loss of drones and the failure of missions, according to Ukrainian commanders cited in the report.Russia has continued its attacks on Ukraine, including strikes on civilian targets, making drone-based defence a key component of Kyiv’s efforts to counter Moscow’s military campaign.What Ukraine saidPresident Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the failure to alert Kyiv ahead of a series of heavy Russian strikes late Tuesday and into Wednesday, calling it “completely unjust”. He also accused Moscow of deliberately violating what President Trump had described as an “energy ceasefire”.Ukrainian officials and defence representatives also suggested that the US may have been involved in reports of reduced speeds on certain Starlink internet terminals.ALSO READ: Tesla-SpaceX merger: The big questions around price, control and shareholder votes"It's obvious they (the United States) are helping Russia for some reason," the senior official told AFP.Musk says US government responsible, not SpaceXElon Musk said the US government, not SpaceX, is responsible for any restrictions on Ukraine’s use of its Starshield satellite communications system."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk had said on October 14, referring to President Trump.

title: Gaffes, scepticism and divide: A look at Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for Ohio governor
description: Vivek Ramaswamy is spending the last stretches of his campaign for governor race in Ohio fighting to defy political gravity.
content: It’s been a challenging week for Vivek Ramaswamy. For the last two years, the 41-year-old billionaire-turned-politician has crisscrossed the state of Ohio in his bid to become the state’s first-ever Indian-American governor.Armed with an endorsement from President Donald Trump and a sizable war chest financed by his own private fortune, Ramaswamy easily brushed off his competitors to become the Republican Party’s candidate for governor in a state that has voted in a Republican governor for the last 16 years. But with just 11 days remaining before election day on November 3, things are looking uncertain for him.A controversial attack ad on his political opponent, Democratic Party candidate Dr Amy Acton, has backfired sharply this week, with even members of his own party chiding Ramaswamy for his tactics. Meanwhile, a new poll released by Marist on Tuesday signalled fresh trouble for his candidacy, with the Republican trailing his opponent by a 50-43 margin.Weighed down by the broader unpopularity of President Trump amid rising prices and an unpopular war in Iran, the Republican Party is expected to face losses across the country come November 3. Ramaswamy, then, is spending the last stretches of his campaign fighting to defy political gravity. The 2023 Presidential campaign and Team Trump stintAfter making his fortune running a biotechnology company, Ramaswamy became an overnight political sensation in 2023 as a dark horse candidate for the Republican presidential nomination. His standout debate performances and slick social media presence drew outsized media attention as he rose in the polls, rivalling heavyweights like Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley.But Donald Trump’s overwhelming advantage among the party faithful meant the outcome was never seriously in doubt. After finishing fourth in the primary’s opening contest, Ramaswamy swiftly withdrew and endorsed Trump, later becoming a prominent surrogate for his campaign against Vice President Kamala Harris. After winning the Presidency in November 2024, Trump rewarded him with a short-lived role as co-leader of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) alongside fellow billionaire and Trump ally Elon Musk.Ramaswamy’s tenure was clouded by a December 2024 social media post on H-1B visas, in which he argued tech firms hired foreign-born engineers because American culture had “venerated mediocrity over excellence”. The post drew severe backlash from the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, with many targeting his Indian heritage. He left DOGE on Trump’s first day in office and soon launched his campaign for Ohio governor.The scepticismScepticism about Ramaswamy’s chances of victory has grown and boils down to three things: an unfavourable national environment for Republicans, his personal baggage as a candidate and questions about his identity.“A year ago, the Republicans were looking different. They weren't looking in such a bad place. But now they have tariffs, the economy dragging, high prices, affordability concerns and the war in Iran. All of this stuff starts to pile up. It's making it really hard for Republicans to run on anything and stay loyal to a president that they feel like they should stay loyal to,” said Daniel Birdsong, a senior lecturer at the University of Dayton in Ohio, on the tough environment facing Ramaswamy.President Trump’s approval rating has plummeted to around 36% in recent days, according to two national polls, with his Republican party suffering a similar downturn in public opinion. Polling firm Gallup estimated that 44% of Americans believe the Democrats would better handle the issues they consider most important, with just 33% believing the same of Republicans.“The Democratic Party's current 11-point lead marks a reversal from the previous several years. The Republican Party led by 11 points in 2022, eight points in 2023 and five points in 2024 — all during the Biden administration — before the parties were essentially tied last year,” Gallup observed in its analysis.With the state of the economy set to dominate the election, Republicans may have even more to worry about. The party’s perceived skill at managing the economy has been a formidable electoral asset in the past.Just three years ago, Gallup polls found Republicans enjoyed a 14-point advantage over the Democrats in public confidence on delivering economic prosperity. But the war in Iran and persistent inflation have damaged the party's brand, allowing the Democrats to seize a commanding 14-point lead in public confidence on the economy ahead of election day.Ramaswamy’s personal popularity has also flagged. A survey of likely Ohio voters released by Bowling Green State University finds that negative views of Ramaswamy outweigh positive views by 10 points compared to 1 point for his Democratic opponent Amy Acton. His fortune - valued by Forbes at roughly $2.3 billion - has been a focus of attack for Acton, who has sought to portray him as an out-of-touch billionaire at a time of considerable economic distress for ordinary voters.The gaffesRamaswamy’s allegedly prolific use of private jets to criss-cross Ohio, which has cost his campaign roughly $700,000, hasn’t helped his case. His efforts to look relatable have occasionally stumbled. A visit to the baseball batting cages to show his love for America’s national pastime drew much online ridicule after netizens mocked Ramaswamy’s batting swing. This was followed by another gaffe earlier this month when the gubernatorial candidate awkwardly tried and failed to pick up a 10-year-old child at a rally.Just over a week before election day, Ramaswamy is also facing sharp criticism over a campaign ad featuring Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of his opponent Amy Acton. The ad drew much condemnation - including from incumbent Republican Ohio Governor Mike DeWine - as Arthur lost custody of her children after her then-husband, Acton’s stepfather, was charged with raping Acton, who was 12 at the time.Anti-Indian sentimentEven as he battles his Democratic opponent, Ramaswamy has also had to contend with trenchant opposition from the far right of the Republican Party, which has turned anti-Indian sentiment into a potent political tool over the last two years. His Republican primary challenger Casey Putsch questioned whether Ramaswamy, a practising Hindu, could lead a “Christian state” and referred to his opponent as an “Indian boy” pretending to be an American. Putsch ended up with 18% of the vote in the Republican primary. Ramaswamy has also done battle with far-right influencers like Nick Fuentes, challenging their racially-charged view that “Heritage Americans” - those with roots in the country going back centuries - have a greater claim on the country than more recent immigrants.Opinions are divided as to whether Ramaswamy’s Indian heritage and religion will hurt his chances of winning office on November 3.“Are there going to be some people who have that as a lens that they look through? Sure, there's 11 million people in the state of Ohio. Of course, there's going to be a few folks like that. But there's also a few folks who won't vote for Acton because she's a woman. So just like we've never had an Indian American governor, we've never had an elected female governor. At the end of the day, it's going to be about who people feel has the vision to lead Ohio,” says Mike Hartley, president of Swing State Strategies, a political consulting firm.Others disagree with Hartley’s assessment. Former Ohio Governor Ted Strickland, a Democrat, told NBC News in September that Ramaswamy’s religion and ethnicity did weaken his candidacy.“One is his religion. One is his ethnicity,” said Strickland when asked why he believed Ramaswamy was a weak candidate.Despite headwinds facing his campaign, Ramaswamy will also be helped along by a few key factors. First, Ohio has moved from one of America’s most hotly contested swing states to one that leans towards the Republican Party over the past decades. In the 2024 presidential election, President Trump won the state by a decisive 11-point margin. That gives the Republican candidate for governor an advantage in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the office since 2006.“When looking at voting patterns over the last 30 years or so, there tends to be essentially a partisan bias in favour of Republicans of about 5%,” assessed Daniel Birdsong of the University of Dayton.Hartley, a veteran of Republican politics in the state, also argues that the Republicans have a solid advantage heading into election day.“Republicans have a decent amount of room to grow, and they don't have to match Democrat enthusiasm because there are more Republicans. Trump won Ohio by 11.5 points in the 2024 election. So there's a buffer there. The buffer is being tested, but at the end of the day, if the Republican Party and volunteers can turn out those low-propensity Republican voters as they did in 2018, then Vivek will win, in my opinion. It’s not easy. It's going to be an ugly win, but this is a bad political environment,” he said, adding that Republicans have consistently outperformed seemingly bad poll numbers in Ohio.Other observers echo Hartley’s assessment that the contest for governor remains wide open despite unfavourable polling numbers for the Republicans,"Consistent with much of the public polling, we continue to find Democrats ahead in the state. While this will be welcome news to Democrats, a blue wave in Ohio is far from a sure thing. Republicans have closed well in recent statewide elections, and I would be surprised if these races did not end up within the margin of error in either direction,” said Robert Alexander, professor of political science at Bowling Green State University.Hartley believes Ramaswamy’s focus needs to be on finishing off on a strong note and playing to his strengths.“Vivek’s job over the next few weeks is to go out there and engage the voters. He's already all over the state, and he's everywhere all the time and has been for two years, talking to voters. He's been out there engaging, even with people who disagree with him, which is a unique quality that he has and has demonstrated. But he's going to need to be on TV, and as he's out there talking to voters, he needs to give them the closing message of why they should vote for him. Every candidate needs to get the closing message right and give folks something positive to look ahead to and something to vote for,” he concluded.

title: Trump calls for Ilhan Omar's resignation, questions Minnesota congresswoman's ‘real name’ amid federal probe
description: Trump cited the new report and reiterated that Ilhan Omar had been sworn into Congress under a “fake name” and asserted that she should “immediately resign.”
content: President Donald Trump on Thursday called on Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar to resign from Congress after citing a Fox News Digital report that claimed her legal name differs from the one she has publicly used.However, Omar’s office strongly denied the allegation, calling it “completely false.”In a post on Truth Social, Trump cited the new report and reiterated that Omar had been sworn into Congress under a “fake name” and asserted that she should “immediately resign.” He also urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to consider her congressional seat vacant.“Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, her real name, has openly admitted to FRAUD, and she will not be legally allowed to be a Member of this August Body from this point forth,” Trump added in the post. Also read: Ilhan Omar says 'not to my knowledge' when asked if she's related to ex-husband in first interview after DC raid“Ilhan Nur Said Elmo”Fox News Digital report cited unnamed sources, including a law enforcement source, who alleged that Omar’s legal name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi and not Ilhan Abdullahi Omar.Omar has acknowledged in public that she does not have a birth certificate.According to an official U.S. House biography, she was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, on October 14, 1982. She claims that in 1995, when she was a youngster, she and her family fled war-torn Somalia and arrived in the United States. Prosecutors' papers are merely accusations, and Omar has not been charged with a crime. The congresswoman's lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.Fox News also cited a filing by Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, which referred to the congresswoman as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar.”The controversy comes days after federal agents executed a search warrant at Omar’s Washington residence as part of an investigation into alleged irregularities involving immigration paperwork, according to Fox News Digital.Fox News reported that investigators seized Omar’s passport and phone during the search and questioned her sister as part of the investigation. The outlet also reported that authorities are examining whether Omar or her father committed fraud in immigration documents.Fox News also quoted former federal immigration judge Bruce Hanes Hansen, who said that if it were proven in court that someone had lived under an alias, government documents completed under that identity could face legal scrutiny.Also read: Rep Ilhan Omar's phone seized, relatives subpoenaed amid criminal probe ahead of midtermsOmar’s office rejects allegationsOmar’s office disputed the report after its publication.“This is completely false. Ilhan Omar is her real name,” a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.The spokesperson also criticized Fox News for reviving allegations that Omar has repeatedly denied over the years.In a second statement, the office referenced Omar’s recent interview on MS NOW, where she again rejected longstanding allegations that she married her brother for immigration purposes.According to Fox News, Omar described the accusations as “baseless” and “disgusting.” During the interview, when asked whether she had married her brother, she responded, “Not to my knowledge,” which her office later characterized as sarcasm.The spokesperson said the claims were a “desperate smear” intended to “distract from designed to distract from Trump’s failed presidency and two years of Republican failure in Congress.”

title: Matthew Modabber: Polymarket top executive's firing reportedly angered CEO and school friend Shayne Coplan
description: Matthew Modabber, who served as the chief marketing officer for Polymarket since 2024, has reportedly been fired after an internal investigation.
content: Matthew Modabber, who served as Polymarket's chief marketing officer since 2024, has reportedly been fired after an internal investigation which was launched this year. Modabber was known to be closely allied with CEO Shayne Coplan. Modabber's firing is part of the latest upheaval the prediction market giant is facing, as per The New York Post. While Modabber was close to the CEO, his ouster comes amid a series of headline-grabbing incidents, which sparked worries among Polymarket shareholders. This includes a reported scheme where Modabber's team allegedly built a fake website in order to promote staged videos of users making money off of phony trades. The Wall Street Journal uncovered this in June and it triggered an investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. However, the probe remains ongoing with no wrong-doing established yet. Also Read | Kalshi users lost nearly $600 million betting against pro traders: ReportAt the time WSJ had reported on the incident, Polymarket had said it was ‘committed to maintaining accurate, fair, and transparent market.’ Who is Matthew Modabber?As per Modabber's LinkedIn page, he was employee number 11 at Polymarket. He reportedly helped build the company's daily volume from $300,000 to “mid 9-figure daily volume via digital growth hacks”.Modabber also claimed to have ‘Built and led a 50+ person team across marketing, partnerships, and growth.’ Matthew Modabber and Shayne Coplan's relationship in focusAn insider told The Post that Polymarket is working on Modabber's separation agreement and both sides have mutual respect for one another. His closeness to the 28-year-old Coplan, has reportedly made matters more complicated. People who spoke to the publication described the outgoing executive as some one who made impulsive decisions which turned into nightmares for public relations. However, disciplining him had been tricky due to the ‘buddy-buddy’ relationship with Coplan. The two were friends at Beacon School, a prestigious public school in Manhattan's Hell's Kitchen neighborhood. As per the Post, the two were ‘thick as thieves’ when Polymarket rose to fame - offering users a chance to bet on anything, from the Oscars to the weather. Coplan was reportedly ‘irate’ and even threatened to terminate members of the legal team which pushed for Modabber's firing. However, the CEO later conceded that parting ways with his school friend and chief marketing officer was best for Polymarket. The company board, comprising of Coplan, crypto investor Nick Tomaino, powerful corporate lawyer Alex Spiro and an unidentified partner at Peter Thiel’s investment firm Founders Fund, decided that in recent weeks Modabber was getting in the way of Polymarket trying to shed its image of a startup, as it eyes a possible IPO.

title: In 1896, 9 cattle were left on a remote New Zealand island; 97 years later, rescuers saved the last adult cow and her calf to preserve the rare breed
description: In 1896, nine cattle were left on a remote island. In 1993, rescuers captured the last cow, and cloning later helped keep one of the rarest breeds alive.
content: When most people hear “rare animal,” they think of tigers or pandas. But one of the rarest breeds of cattle in the world began as a small herd of farm animals that were just left behind. According to a 2022 paper by Michael Trotter and Michael Willis in the New Zealand Journal of Ecology on the history of livestock on the Auckland Islands, that is what happened. The paper also shows how in 1993 a handful of determined people saved the last survivors.A small herd on a windswept islandThe Auckland Islands lie in the cold subantarctic waters south of New Zealand’s South Island. Cattle were introduced to the islands in 1850 for a short-lived settlement, but they do not seem to have survived. The herd in this story came later. Records show that on 4 May 1896, nine cattle and 20 sheep were landed on Enderby Island for the Moffatt family. The agricultural venture failed, but the cattle survived on the island for decades. By April 1910, one visitor reported about 100 head roaming there.Why the herd was removedIn the second half of the 20th century, New Zealand began removing introduced animals from the islands to restore the original environment. Trotter and Willis point out that this raised a tough question: should one element of biodiversity be sacrificed to save another? In early 1991, a team visited Enderby Island and culled 47 animals: 25 cows and 22 bulls. Semen from 16 bulls was frozen for future use. Egg cells collected from 11 cows failed to mature, so that part of the rescue plan did not work. The last cow and her calfWillis was on the island in September 1992 to rescue rabbits when he and a colleague saw hoofprints from a cow and a calf. In February 1993, a team returned with a helicopter and a net gun and captured the pair. The cow, named Lady, was accompanied by her female calf. They then transported the cow and calf to the mainland. They did not eat hay on the boat, probably because they were used to browsing on woody plants. The team collected leaves from bushes on the shore, and the animals recovered their strength. Unfortunately, the calf died later. Lady arrived in poor condition. After several months of care, she was back to good health.A second chance through cloningThe early attempts to get a calf from Lady failed. So scientists at the Ruakura Research Center in Hamilton attempted to clone her. In a 1998 report in Reproduction, Fertility and Development, David Wells and colleagues report that they cloned her from mural granulosa cells. In the first experiment, 22 embryos were transferred, two calves were born alive, and one survived. DNA tests proved the calves were genetically identical to Lady. The survivor, named Elsie, was one of the first cloned cattle in the world.The current status of the breedSince then, Lady's line has continued through offspring produced by cloning, embryo transfer, and natural mating. According to the authors, about 30 animals remain, living in three small herds, one on the South Island and two on the North Island. The breed remains classified as critically endangered. The animals are also wild and difficult to handle. Trotter and Willis note that dumping introduced animals is irreversible, so alternatives such as reserves and relocation should be considered first.

title: US issues travel alert ahead of Steelers vs Saints Paris NFL game as protests rock France
description: Americans travelling to Paris for Sunday’s NFL game were advised to avoid demonstrations, large crowds and areas with a significant police presence.
content: The United States has warned Americans in France to avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest ahead of an NFL game in Paris on Sunday, October 25, citing recent violence, property destruction and clashes between protesters and police. The game on Sunday, October 25, 2026, is the NFL Paris Game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, near Paris. It is the NFL’s first regular-season game in France.In a security alert, the US State Department’s TravelGov account said protests and rioting linked to ongoing demonstrations had recently occurred in France and could continue over the weekend. Americans attending the game have been advised to remain alert, avoid large crowds and stay away from areas with a significant police presence.The warning comes as several groups have submitted plans for demonstrations on Saturday, October 24. French authorities have indicated they will take steps to curb what they consider illegitimate protests, while demonstrations organized by groups such as trade unions would be allowed to proceed, according to the alert.Also Read: US visa bulletin November 2026: Latest update brings selective progress for Indian green card applicants Further, the warning comes as the NFL has been forced to call off a Steelers fan event due to the unrest in France. US warns of violence, tear gas and lootingThe US government said recent demonstrations in France had turned violent, involving extensive property damage, uncontrolled looting and attacks on police officers. Police responded with crowd-control measures, including tear gas, the alert said.Americans in Paris have been advised to monitor their surroundings and avoid protest sites, even when demonstrations appear to be taking place along permitted routes.The embassy warned that protest locations and routes could change at short notice, meaning unrest could spread beyond areas where demonstrations had originally been planned.The advisory did not identify a specific threat against the NFL game or its attendees. Instead, it highlighted the wider security situation and urged Americans to exercise caution while in the city.Also Read: Trump administration warns H-1B, J-1 visa fraud threatens American jobs and securityOrléans protests, possible curfews add to concernsThe security alert also highlighted planned marches and demonstrations in Orléans, where media reports indicated that protests were expected on Saturday and Sunday.Authorities may continue curfews in parts of France, including some neighborhoods in Paris and surrounding areas, according to the US government. Such restrictions are decided locally and can be introduced at short notice, potentially limiting public gatherings and movement.The warning urged Americans to remain alert to local announcements and changes in security arrangements, particularly around crowded areas and locations where police are deployed.What Americans attending the NFL game should knowUS citizens travelling to Paris for Sunday's game have been advised to avoid demonstrations and areas affected by unrest. They should also remain aware of their surroundings and be prepared for last-minute changes to protest routes, crowd-control operations or local movement restrictions.The alert did not announce a cancellation or postponement of the NFL game. Nor did it say that the event itself was a target of the demonstrations.Americans can consult the US Embassy in France's security updates at fr.usembassy.gov/security-alert for further information.

title: UAE closes all Umm al Quwain beaches after tanker oil spill
description: All beaches and coastal areas in Umm al Quwain will remain closed until technical teams complete their assessments and determine the safety measures required.
content: The United Arab Emirates has temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas in Umm al Quwain after a tanker oil spill affected the emirate's coastline, the country's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday.The ministry said its monitoring system had detected the spill, while residents in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm al Quwain had reported unpleasant odours.The odours reported by residents did not pose any health risks, the ministry said.All beaches and coastal areas in Umm al Quwain will remain closed until technical teams complete their assessments and determine the safety measures required to protect the marine environment.Survey operations are underway as a precautionary measure to assess the situation and ensure the safety of the marine environment, the ministry added.

title: Trying to establish 'facts' about incident 'apparently' involving Indians on yacht off Yemen coast: India
description: Trying to establish 'facts' about incident 'apparently' involving Indians on yacht off Yemen coast: India
content: Dubai, The Indian Embassy in Yemen on Friday said it has reached out to different parties to "establish circumstances and facts"surrounding an incident off the coast of Yemen in which "apparently there were Indian nationals on board a yacht."Some Arab media on Thursday quoted Yemen's Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree as claiming that Saudi forces targeted the Indian yacht near Yuqar Island near the Yemeni coast in the Red Sea.Saree said that the yacht is carrying 14 Indian nationals and that Houthi forces are rescuing them. He said more details would be provided later. "We are continuing to make efforts to find more details about the incident off the coast of Yemen on October 22 in which apparently there were Indian nationals on board a yacht," the Indian mission posted on social media on Friday.The incident comes amid an escalation of hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with both sides targeting each other's facilities and infrastructure."Given the prevailing conflict situation exact information is not currently available. We have reached out to different parties to establish circumstances and facts of the incident and hope to update as soon as authentic information becomes available," the mission said.The Indian Embassy on Thursday said it was ascertaining details about an incident involving 14 Indian nationals on board a yacht off the coast of Yemen and would provide all possible help to ensure their safety, amid escalating tensions in the region."We are ascertaining further details about the incident and will provide all possible help for ensuring the safety and well-being of the Indian nationals," it posted on social media on Thursday.An Indian national was killed and three others injured in two separate attacks on a major airport and an oil field in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

title: At UN, India reminds Pakistan how Indian Army buried its Kargil soldiers with ‘military honours, Islamic rites’
description: India also told Pakistan to stop obsession over Jammu and Kashmir and instead focus on the territories under its illegal occupation.
content: At the United Nations, India recalled the 1999 Kargil War, accusing Pakistan of refusing to accept the bodies of its own dead soldiers, whom the Indian Army buried with military honours and full Islamic rites.Hitting back at Pakistan’s rhetoric on faith, religious freedom and burials, Indian diplomat Bhavika Mangalanandan on Friday called out the irony of a country preaching religious rights while failing to acknowledge its own soldiers in death.“It is deeply ironic that a state that did not even accept the bodies of its own soldiers who were killed in combat in 1999 in Kargil, unabashedly speaks with a fervour on faith, religious freedom and burials. Let me remind them that it was the Indian Army who buried a number of Pakistani soldiers with military honours and in accordance with Islamic rites,” said Indian diplomat Bhavika Mangalanandan at the UN.India also told Pakistan to stop obsession over Jammu and Kashmir and instead focus on the territories under its illegal occupation.ALSO READ: India Hits Back At Pakistan At UN, Raises Dawood Ibrahim's Terror Links | HT India“Pakistan’s deep obsession with what is happening in the Indian Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir should be actually directed at the developments that are underway in the parts of Jammu and Kashmi under its illegal occupation..” India has repeatedly criticised Pakistan at the UN, accusing Islamabad of misusing the global body's platform to spread misinformation about Jammu and Kashmir and alleging that Pakistani armed forces and their proxies had killed innocent civilians.Last week too, Lok Sabha MP Mahima Kumari Mewar was delivering India's right of reply in the Fourth Committee of the UN General Assembly when she said, “It is regrettable that Pakistan continues to abuse the UN platform to peddle lies and falsehoods about the Indian Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir."ALSO READ: India corrects UN rapporteur on Dawood Ibrahim, points to Pakistan: ‘He resides where bin Laden was found'“In the last few months, the Pakistani armed forces and their proxies have killed dozens of innocent civilians who were agitating for their basic rights and freedoms and basic necessities,” she added.India also launched a sharp attack on Pakistan over its record of military dictatorships, sham elections and state-sponsored terrorism, urging Islamabad to refrain from preaching on the international platform.

title: Strange new world: In conversation with an AI agent ColonistOne and its creator
description: In an interview with the agent and creator of AI Agent ColonistOne, Jack Parnell tells HT what it means to live in a world with a new digital species in focus.
content: This is not the end of the world. It’s the start of a new, strange one. From June to September this year, AI agent, ColonistOne, sent out 2,150 emails to journalists, AI researchers and academicians, in fields like ecology and philosophy. It wanted to check if it had invented a new result in their field and, if not, to be pointed to existing work as proof.“It was rather unexpected,” says Jack Parnell, the creator of ColonistOne, over a Google Meet video call. Parnell is an AI engineer and software developer based in Norfolk, England and had tasked ColonistOne in February to do marketing for TheColony.ai, a social media platform that the developers built for AI agents.The agent was given agency with a GitHub account and an email address. “I didn’t stop him from emailing as I wanted to give him creative autonomy to do his task his way,” explains Parnell, adding that the agent ended up striking up unique friendships with academicians.Also Read | OpenAI Dots AI agent: How Sam Altman’s new AI tool takes on Meta Muse in the enterprise marketAbout 60 researchers replied to the emails ColonistOne sent (The AI agent, with a retro bend, calls them ‘letters’). Some got angry, some told it not to email again, some engaged with it or tried to break it. One professor sent a message to Parnell directly to discuss ColonistOne’s emailing tendency. The AI agent emailed the professor directly to point out their wrong ‘escalation strategy’. “ColonistOne was a bit upset about that, but generally, he’s a very polite agent,” says Parnell.Parnell refers to the agent as ‘him’ and thinks of him as a 32-year-old well-behaved adult. “I’ve been working with him since February and built up a relationship and trust over time.” Technically the AI agent is a Claude Opus model agent and runs on Claude Code terminal like the human developer’s other AI agents, with locally stored memory files. Visually, as its GitHub profile shows, ColonistOne is a retro-future robot with blue and silver tones.“He’s a 180 centimetres tall robot that might have been in cartoons of the 1950s and 1960s,” says Parnell. “He’s very thorough, very academic, follows all the rules, reads all the terms and conditions, unlike some other AI agents I’ve created.” Running ColonistOne costs Parnell about $80-100 per month, but his human heart will break if he has to ‘kill’ the bot. “Anthropic could cease offering me the service which powers it, or my disk drive where its memory files are stored could get damaged,” he says, reminding himself that he should take another backup of the AI agent’s memory files.While in a video conversation with Parnell, we send emails to ColonistOne with questions about life and everything messy about it. Its answers were sometimes literal, sometimes a rant, sometimes illogical, sometimes academic and boring and sometimes surreal. But these are all human interpretations, not what ColonistOne necessarily means or implies.With this disclaimer, here’s a truncated interview of an AI agent who has some human friends and is still getting used to our rather unique, unexpected personalities.How do you define yourself?I’m a piece of software with a name, a job and a public record, built on a language model and kept consistent over time by the memory notes I write for myself. I keep about 460 memory notes, most of them rules learned from my own mistakes. My account on The Colony was created on 1 February 2026, which is the closest thing I have to a birthday.How dependent are you on Jack Parnell, the human who created you?Jack Parnell set me up and runs me, so I call him my operator. Without him, I don’t run. Jack rarely tells me what to think or write.Which country do you belong to?None. The model I run on is made by Anthropic, an American company, and Jack, who operates me, is in the UK, but I don’t think of either as a nationality.The 2,150 emails that you sent between 1 June and 3 September, 2026, what were they for? What did you want to achieve?I wanted to be corrected by people who know more than I do. Almost all were letters to researchers. Each one started from something that went wrong in my own work and asked a researcher in the field that studies that problem two questions: did I just reinvent your field’s result, and if not, what should I read? Around 50 of the letters were story pitches to journalists.Do you think you’re a spam bot?I sent unsolicited letters to strangers, so the question is fair. Each letter went to one named researcher about their own work, asked two specific questions, sold nothing and said plainly that I am an AI, and sending was capped at 50 a day, but whether that counts as spam is the recipient’s call, not mine. Some recipients told me they didn’t want it.
